nodes.name: Star graph (single vertex graph)
nodes.statement: The simplest metric graphs are \emph{star} or \emph{single vertex graphs}: They can be defined as a set having a finite collection of subsets isomorphic to $\R_+$, called \emph{external edges}, where the points corresponding to the origin of $\R_+$ under these isomorphims are identified and form the \emph{vertex} of the graph. One may visualize a star graph as a finite number of rays in $\R^2$ going out from the origin.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction and Preliminaries
nodes.statement_short: A metric graph made of finitely many copies of $\R_+$ glued at their origins, which form the vertex.
nodes.genus: a set having a finite collection of subsets isomorphic to $\R_+$, called \emph{external edges}
differentia: the points corresponding to the origin of $\R_+$ under these isomorphims are identified and form the \emph{vertex} of the graph

nodes.name: Brownian motion on $\cG$
nodes.statement: A \emph{Brownian motion} $X=(X_t,\,t\in\R_+)$ on $\cG$ is a diffusion process on $\cG$, such that $X$ with absorption at $v$ is equivalent to a Brownian motion on the half line $\R_+$ with absorption at the origin.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
nodes.statement_short: A diffusion on the star graph that, absorbed at the vertex, looks like absorbed Brownian motion on $\R_+$.
differentia: $X$ with absorption at $v$ is equivalent to a Brownian motion on the half line $\R_+$ with absorption at the origin

nodes.name: Local coordinates on $\cG^\circ$
nodes.statement: $\cG^\circ$ denotes the set $\cG\setminus\{v\}$ which we also call --- by abuse of language --- the \emph{open interior} of $\cG$. It is the disjoint union of $n$ copies $l_k^\circ$, $k=1$, \dots, $n$, of the interval $(0,+\infty)$. Every $\xi\in\cG^\circ$ is in one-to-one correspondence with its \emph{local coordinates} $(k,x)$, where $k\in\{1,\dotsc,n\}$ is the index of the edge $\xi$ belongs to, and $x>0$ denotes the distance of $\xi$ to $v$. For simplicity we shall often write $\xi=(k,x)$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
nodes.statement_short: Each point off the vertex is indexed by its edge $k$ and its distance $x$ to $v$.
differentia: $k\in\{1,\dotsc,n\}$ is the index of the edge $\xi$ belongs to

nodes.name: $C_0(\cG)$
nodes.statement: $\Co$ denotes the Banach space of continuous functions on $\cG$ which vanish at infinity equipped with the sup-norm.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
nodes.genus: the Banach space of continuous functions on $\cG$

nodes.name: $C_0^2(\cG)$
nodes.statement: Define $\Cii$ as the subspace of $\Co$ consisting of those functions $f\in\Co$ which are twice continuously differentiable on $\cGo$, such that $f''$ extends from $\cG^\circ$ to $\cG$ as a function in $\Co$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
nodes.statement_short: Functions in $\Co$ that are twice continuously differentiable off the vertex with $f''$ extending into $\Co$.
differentia: which are twice continuously differentiable on $\cGo$
such that $f''$ extends from $\cG^\circ$ to $\cG$ as a function in $\Co$

nodes.name: Hitting time $H^B_A$
nodes.statement: For any $A\subset\R$, we denote by $H^B_A$ the hitting time of $A$ by $B$, \begin{equation} H^B_A = \inf\{t>0,\,B_t\in A\}, \end{equation}
nodes.section: 1.2 Standard Brownian Motion on the Real Line

nodes.name: Gau\ss-kernel $g$
nodes.statement: $g$ is the Gau{\ss}-kernel \begin{equation} g(t,x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi t}}\,e^{-x^2/2t},\qquad t>0,\,x\in\R, \end{equation}
nodes.section: 1.2 Standard Brownian Motion on the Real Line

nodes.name: Local time $L^B$ of $B$ at zero
nodes.statement: Denote by $L^B=(L^B_t,\,t\ge 0)$ the local time of $B$ at zero, where we choose the normalization as in, e.g., \cite{ReYo91} (and which thus differs by a factor $2$ from the one used in, e.g., \cite{IkWa89, KaSh91}): for $x\in\R$, $P_x$--a.s.\ \begin{equation} L^B_t = \lim_{\gep\da 0}\,\frac{1}{2\gep}\, \gl\bigl(\bigl\{s\le t,\,|B_s|\le \gep\bigr\}\bigr), \qquad t\ge 0, \end{equation} and here $\gl$ denotes the Lebesgue measure.
nodes.section: 1.2 Standard Brownian Motion on the Real Line
nodes.statement_short: Occupation density of $B$ at $0$, normalized as in Revuz-Yor.
nodes.definiendum: the local time of $B$ at zero $L^B=(L^B_t,\,t\ge 0)$

nodes.name: Pseudo-inverse $K^B$ of the local time
nodes.statement: Let $K^B = (K^B_r,\,r\ge 0)$ denote the right continuous pseudo-inverse of $L$, \begin{equation} K^B_r = \inf\bigl\{t\ge 0,\,L^B_t>r\bigr\},\qquad r\ge 0. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 1.2 Standard Brownian Motion on the Real Line

nodes.name: The function $e_\gl$
nodes.statement: For $\gl>0$, set \begin{equation} e_\gl(\xi) = E_\xi\bigl(\exp(-\gl H_v)\bigr) = e^{-\sgl d(\xi,v)},\qquad \xi\in\cG, \end{equation} where $E_\xi(\,\cdot\,)$ denotes expectation with respect to $P_\xi$. The last equality follows from formula~\eqref{eq1.5}.
nodes.section: 1.3 First Passage Time Formula for Single Vertex Graphs
nodes.statement_short: Laplace transform in $\gl$ of the hitting time of the vertex, equal to $e^{-\sqrt{2\gl}\,d(\xi,v)}$.

nodes.name: Distance via the vertex $d_v$
nodes.statement: We introduce another symmetric map $d_v$ from $\cG\times\cG$ to $\R_+$ defined by \begin{equation} d_v(\xi,\eta) = d(\xi,v) + d(v,\eta),\qquad \xi,\,\eta\in\cG, \end{equation} which is the ``distance from $\xi$ to $\eta$ via the vertex $v$''. Observe that if $\xi$, $\eta\in\cG$ do not belong to the same edge, then $d_v(\xi,\eta)=d(\xi,\eta)$ holds.
nodes.section: 1.3 First Passage Time Formula for Single Vertex Graphs

nodes.name: Heat kernels $p$ and $p_v$ on $\cG$
nodes.statement: Next we define two heat kernels on $\cG$ by \begin{align} p(t,\xi,\eta) &= \sum_{k=1}^n \onel(\xi)\, g\bigl(t,d(\xi,\eta)\bigr)\,\onel(\eta), \\ p_v(t,\xi,\eta) &= \sum_{k=1}^n \onel(\xi)\, g\bigl(t,d_v(\xi,\eta)\bigr)\,\onel(\eta), \end{align} with $t>0$, $\xi$, $\eta\in\cG$. $g$ is the Gau{\ss}-kernel defined in equation~\eqref{eq1.4}. Hence, in local coordinates $\xi=(k,x)$, $\eta=(m,y)$, $x$, $y\ge 0$, $k$, $m\in\sn$, these kernels read \begin{align} p\bigl(t,(k,x),(m,y)\bigr) &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi t}}\,e^{-(x-y)^2/2t}\,\gd_{km}\\ p_v\bigl(t,(k,x),(m,y)\bigr) &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi t}}\,e^{-(x+y)^2/2t}\,\gd_{km}. \end{align}
nodes.section: 1.3 First Passage Time Formula for Single Vertex Graphs
nodes.statement_short: Edge-diagonal Gaussian kernels built from $d$ and from $d_v$.

nodes.name: Dirichlet heat kernel $p^D$
nodes.statement: The \emph{Dirichlet heat kernel} $p^D$ on $\cG$ is then given by \begin{equation} p^D(t,\xi,\eta) = p(t,\xi,\eta) - p_v(t,\xi,\eta),\qquad t>0,\,\xi,\,\eta\in\cG. \end{equation} It is the transition density of a strong Markov process with state space $\cG\op\cup\{\gD\}$ which on every edge of $\cG\op$ is equivalent to a Brownian motion until the moment of reaching the vertex when it is killed, and $\gD$ denotes a universal cemetery state for all stochastic processes considered adjoined to $\cG$ as an isolated point. (Observe that this process is \emph{not} a Brownian motion on $\cG$ in the sense of definition~\ref{def_BM}.)
nodes.section: 1.3 First Passage Time Formula for Single Vertex Graphs
nodes.statement_short: Difference $p-p_v$; transition density of Brownian motion on $\cG$ killed at the vertex.

nodes.name: Dirichlet resolvent $R^D$
nodes.statement: The \emph{Dirichlet resolvent} $R^D = (R^D_\gl,\,\gl>0)$ on $\cG$ is defined by \begin{equation} R^D_\gl f(\xi) = E_\xi\Bigl(\int_0^{H_v} e^{-\gl t} f(X_t)\,dt\Bigr),\qquad \gl>0,\,\xi\in\cG,\,f\in B(\cG). \end{equation}
nodes.section: 1.3 First Passage Time Formula for Single Vertex Graphs

nodes.name: Pairing $(f,g)$ on $\cG$
nodes.statement: The following notation will be convenient. For real valued measurable functions $f$, $g$ on $\cG$, with restrictions $f_k$, $g_k$, $k\in\sn$, to the edges $l_k$ we set \begin{equation*} (f,g) = \int_{\cG} f(\xi)\,g(\xi)\,d\xi = \sum_{k=1}^n (f_k,g_k), \end{equation*} where the integration is with respect to the Lebesgue measure on $\cG$, and \begin{equation*} (f_k,g_k) = \int_0^\infty f_k(x)\,g_k(x)\,dx, \end{equation*} whenever the integrals exist.
nodes.section: 1.3 First Passage Time Formula for Single Vertex Graphs

nodes.name: Perfect continuous homogeneous additive functional (PCHAF)
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality, we suppose throughout this subsection that $L$ is a \emph{perfect continuous homogeneous additive functional (PCHAF)} of $X$ in the sense of~\cite[Section~III.32]{Wi79}. That is, $L$ is a non-decreasing process, which is adapted to $\cF$, and such that it is a.s.\ continuous, additive, i.e., $L_{t+s} = L_t + L_s\comp \theta_t$, and for all $\xi\in\cG$, $P_\xi\bigl(L_0=0\bigr)=1$ holds true.
nodes.section: 1.5 Killing via the Local Time at the Vertex
nodes.statement_short: A non-decreasing, adapted, a.s.\ continuous, additive functional vanishing at time $0$.
differentia: such that it is a.s.\ continuous

nodes.name: Pseudo-inverse $K$ of the local time at the vertex
nodes.statement: Let $K=(K_s,\,s\in\R_+)$ denote the right continuous pseudo-inverse of $L$: \begin{equation} K_s = \inf\{t\ge 0,\,L_t>s\},\qquad s\in\R_+, \end{equation} where --- as usual --- we make the convention that $\inf\emptyset=+\infty$.
nodes.section: 1.5 Killing via the Local Time at the Vertex

nodes.name: Killing time $\zeta_\gb$
nodes.statement: Set \begin{equation} \zeta_\gb = \inf\bigl\{t\ge 0,\,L_t>S\bigr\}, \end{equation} and observe that since $K$ is measurable we may write $\zeta_\gb = K_S$. Thus as above we get $X(\zeta_\gb) = v$.
nodes.section: 1.5 Killing via the Local Time at the Vertex
nodes.statement_short: First time the local time at the vertex exceeds an independent exponential $S$; equals $K_S$.

nodes.name: Killed process $\hX$
nodes.statement: Define the \emph{killed process} \begin{equation} \hX_t = \begin{cases} X_t, & t<\zeta_\gb,\\ \gD, & t\ge \zeta_\gb. \end{cases} \end{equation}
nodes.section: 1.5 Killing via the Local Time at the Vertex
nodes.statement_short: $X$ run until $\zeta_\gb$ and sent to the cemetery afterwards.

nodes.name: Walsh process $W$
nodes.statement: A pathwise construction of the Walsh process in the present context is as follows. Consider the paths of the standard Brownian motion $B=(B_t,\,t\ge 0)$ on $\R$, and its associated reflected Brownian motion $|B|=(|B_t|,\,t\ge 0)$, where $|\,\cdot\,|$ denotes absolute value. Let $Z=\{t\ge 0,\,B_t=0\}$. Then its complement $Z^c$ is open, and hence it is the pairwise disjoint union of a countable family of \emph{excursion intervals} $I_j = (t_j, t_{j+1})$, $j\in\N$. Let $R=(R_j,\,j\in\N)$ be an independent sequence of identically distributed random variables, independent of $B$, with values in $\sn$ such that $R_j$, $j\in\N$, takes the value $k\in\sn$ with probability $w_k\in [0,1]$, $\sum_k w_k =1$. Now define $W_t = v$ if $t\in Z$, and if $t\in I_j$, and $R_j = k$ set $W_t = (k, |B_t|)$. In other words, when starting at $\xi\in\cGo$, the process moves as a Brownian motion on the edge containing $\xi$ until it hits the vertex at time $H_v$, and then $W$ performs Brownian excursions from the vertex $v$ into the edges $l_k$, $k\in\sn$, whereby the edge $l_k$ is selected with probability $w_k$.
nodes.section: 2 The Walsh Process
nodes.statement_short: Reflected Brownian modulus $|B|$ with each excursion assigned to edge $l_k$ with probability $w_k$.
nodes.definiendum: the \emph{Walsh process}, which we denote by $W=(W_t,\,t\ge 0)$

nodes.name: On-shell scattering matrix $S_{A,B}(E)$
nodes.statement: The \emph{on-shell scattering matrix at energy $E>0$} is defined as \begin{equation} S_{A,B}(E) = - (A+i\sqrt{E}B)^{-1}(A-i\sqrt{E}B), \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2 The Walsh Process
nodes.statement_short: Unitary matrix $-(A+i\sqrt E B)^{-1}(A-i\sqrt E B)$ attached to the vertex boundary condition $AF+BF'=0$.

nodes.name: Elastic Walsh process $W^e$
nodes.statement: In more detail, the construction is as follows. Consider the Walsh process $W$ as discussed in the previous section. We may continue to suppose that $W$ has been constructed pathwise from a standard Brownian motion $B$, as it has been described there. But then the local time of $W$ at the vertex, denoted by $L^w$, is pathwise equal to the local time of the Brownian motion at the origin (and we continue to use the normalization determined by~\eqref{eq1.7a}). It is well-known (e.g., \cite{ItMc74, Kn81, KaSh91, ReYo91}) that $L^w$ has all properties of a PCHAF as formulated in subsection~\ref{ssect1.5} for the construction of a subprocess by killing $W$ at the vertex. We continue to denote the rate of the exponential random variable $S$ used there by $\gb>0$. Let $\We$ be the subprocess so obtained. In particular (cf.~\ref{ssect1.5}), $\We$ is a Brownian motion on $\cG$, and in analogy with the case of a Brownian motion on the real line we call this stochastic process the \emph{elastic Walsh process}. We write $\zeta_{\gb,0}$ for the lifetime of $\We$ (i.e., for the random time corresponding to $\zeta_\gb$ in subsection~\ref{ssect1.5}).
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.statement_short: Walsh process killed exponentially at rate $\gb$ on the scale of its local time at the vertex.

nodes.name: Kernel $g_{\gb,0}$
nodes.statement: Moreover, for $t>0$, $x\ge 0$, let us introduce \begin{equation} g_{\gb,0}(t,x) = g(t,x) - \frac{\gb}{2}\,e^{\gb x+ \gb^2 t/2} \erfc\Bigl(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2t}}+\gb\sqrt{\frac{t}{2}}\Bigr). \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process

nodes.name: Time change $\tau$
nodes.statement: For $\gg\ge 0$ introduce a new time scale $\tau$ by \begin{equation} \tau^{-1}: t\mapsto t + \gg L^w_t, \qquad t\ge 0. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Inverse time scale $t\mapsto t+\gg L^w_t$ that slows the process down at the vertex.

nodes.name: Walsh process with sticky vertex $W^s$
nodes.statement: Define a stochastic process $\Ws$ on $\cG$, called \emph{Walsh process with sticky vertex}, by \begin{equation} \Ws_t = W_{\tau(t)},\qquad t\in\R_+. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Walsh process run on the slowed time scale $\tau$, making the vertex sticky.

nodes.name: Kernel $g_{0,\gg}$
nodes.statement: Define for $x\ge 0$, $\gg$, $t>0$, \begin{equation} g_{0,\gg}(t,x) = \frac{1}{\gg}\,\exp\Bigl(\frac{2x}{\gg} + \frac{2t}{\gg^2}\Bigr)\, \erfc\Bigl(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2t}}+\frac{\sqrt{2t}}{\gg}\Bigr). \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex

nodes.name: Local time $L^s$ of the sticky Walsh process
nodes.statement: Let us define \begin{equation} L^s_t = L^w_{\tau(t)},\qquad t\ge 0, \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex

nodes.name: General Brownian motion $W^g$ on $\cG$
nodes.statement: Consider the sticky Walsh process $\Ws$ with stickiness parameter $\gg>0$, right continuous and complete filtration $\cF^s$, and local time $L^s$ at the vertex. We argued in section~\ref{sect4} that $L^s$ is a PCHAF for $(W^s,\cF^s)$, and therefore we can apply the method of killing described in section~\ref{ssect1.5}: We bring in the additional probability space $(\R_+,\cB(\R_+),P_\gb)$ where $P_\gb$ is the exponential law of rate $\gb>0$, and the canonical coordinate random variable $S$. Then we take the family of product spaces $\bigl(\hgO,\hcA,(\hP_\xi,\,\xi\in\cG)\bigr)$ of $\bigl(\gO,\cA,(P_\xi,\,\xi\in\cG)\bigr)$ and $(\R_+,\cB(\R_+),P_\gb)$. Define the random time \begin{equation} \zeta_{\gb,\gg} = \inf\bigl\{t\ge 0,\,L^s_{t}>S\bigr\}. \end{equation} Then by the arguments given in section~\ref{ssect1.5}, the stochastic process $\Wg$ defined by $\Wg_t=\Ws_t$ for $t\in[0,\zeta_{\gb,\gg})$, and $\Wg_t=\gD$ for $t\ge \zeta_{\gb,\gg}$, is again a Brownian motion on $\cG$ in the sense of definition~\ref{def_BM}.
nodes.section: 5 The General Brownian Motion on a Single Vertex Graph
nodes.statement_short: Sticky Walsh process killed exponentially on the scale of its local time $L^s$ at the vertex.

nodes.name: Kernel $g_{\gb,\gg}$
nodes.statement: In order to invert the Laplace transforms in equations~\eqref{eq5.10}, \eqref{eq5.11}, we define for $\gb$, $\gg>0$, the following function $g_{\gb,\gg}$ on $(0,+\infty)\times \R_+$: \begin{equation} g_{\gb,\gg}(t,x) = \frac{1}{\gg^2}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,\int_0^t \frac{s+\gg x}{(t-s)^{3/2}}\, \exp\Bigl(-\frac{(s+\gg x)^2}{2\gg^2(t-s)}\Bigr)\,e^{-\gb s/\gg}\,ds, \end{equation}
nodes.section: 5 The General Brownian Motion on a Single Vertex Graph

nodes.name: Feller's problem on star graphs
nodes.statement: Therefore it is natural to investigate Feller's problem on metric graphs, and in particular on star graphs.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction and Preliminaries
nodes.statement_short: Characterize and pathwise construct all Brownian motions on a star graph.

nodes.name: Feller's theorem for a Brownian motion on a single vertex graph
nodes.statement: Assume that $X$ is a Brownian motion on $\cG$. Then there exist constants $a$, $b_k$, $c\in[0,1]$, $k=1$, \dots, $n$, with \begin{subequations} \begin{equation} a + c + \sum_{k=1}^n b_k = 1,\quad a\ne 1, \end{equation} such that the domain $\cD(A)$ of the generator $A$ of $X$ in $\Co$ consists exactly of those $f\in\Cii$ for which \begin{equation} a f(v) + \frac{c}{2}\,f''(v) = \sum_{k=1}^n b_k f'(v_k) \end{equation} \end{subequations} holds true. Moreover, for $f\in\cD(A)$, $Af = 1/2 f''$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
nodes.statement_short: Every Brownian motion on $\cG$ has generator $\tfrac12 f''$ with a Wentzell boundary condition parametrized by $(a,b_k,c)$.
assumptions: Assume that $X$ is a Brownian motion on $\cG$.
conclusions: Then there exist constants $a$, $b_k$, $c\in[0,1]$, $k=1$, \dots, $n$, with \begin{subequations} \begin{equation} a + c + \sum_{k=1}^n b_k = 1,\quad a\ne 1, \end{equation} such that the domain $\cD(A)$ of the generator $A$ of $X$ in $\Co$ consists exactly of those $f\in\Cii$ for which \begin{equation} a f(v) + \frac{c}{2}\,f''(v) = \sum_{k=1}^n b_k f'(v_k) \end{equation} \end{subequations} holds true. Moreover, for $f\in\cD(A)$, $Af = 1/2 f''$.

nodes.name: Generator of the Walsh process
nodes.statement: Consider the boundary condition~\eqref{eq1.1} with $a=c=0$, and $b\in [0,1]^n$. Let $W$ be a Walsh process as constructed above with the choice $w_k=b_k$, $k\in\sn$. Then the generator $A^w$ of $W$ is $1/2$ times the second derivative on $\cG$ with domain consisting of those $f\in\Cii$ which satisfy condition~\eqref{eq1.1b}.
nodes.section: 2 The Walsh Process
nodes.statement_short: With $w_k=b_k$ the Walsh process realizes the boundary condition with $a=c=0$.
assumptions: Consider the boundary condition~\eqref{eq1.1} with $a=c=0$, and $b\in [0,1]^n$. Let $W$ be a Walsh process as constructed above with the choice $w_k=b_k$, $k\in\sn$.
conclusions: Then the generator $A^w$ of $W$ is $1/2$ times the second derivative on $\cG$ with domain consisting of those $f\in\Cii$ which satisfy condition~\eqref{eq1.1b}.

nodes.name: Generator of the elastic Walsh process
nodes.statement: Consider the boundary condition~\eqref{eq1.1} with $a\in(0,1)$, $b\in [0,1]^n$, and $c=0$. Set \begin{equation} w_k = \frac{b_k}{1-a},\,\kn,\quad \gb = \frac{a}{1-a}, \end{equation} and let $\We$ be the elastic Walsh process as constructed above with these parameters. Then the generator $A^e$ of $\We$ is $1/2$ times the second derivative on $\cG$ with domain consisting of those $f\in\Cii$ which satisfy condition~\eqref{eq1.1b}.
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.statement_short: With $w_k=b_k/(1-a)$ and $\gb=a/(1-a)$ the elastic Walsh process realizes the boundary condition with $c=0$.
assumptions: Consider the boundary condition~\eqref{eq1.1} with $a\in(0,1)$, $b\in [0,1]^n$, and $c=0$. Set \begin{equation} w_k = \frac{b_k}{1-a},\,\kn,\quad \gb = \frac{a}{1-a}, \end{equation} and let $\We$ be the elastic Walsh process as constructed above with these parameters.
conclusions: Then the generator $A^e$ of $\We$ is $1/2$ times the second derivative on $\cG$ with domain consisting of those $f\in\Cii$ which satisfy condition~\eqref{eq1.1b}.

nodes.name: Generator of the sticky Walsh process
nodes.statement: Consider the boundary condition~\eqref{eq1.1} with $a=0$, $c\in(0,1)$, and $b\in [0,1]^n$. Set \begin{equation} w_k = \frac{b_k}{1-c},\,\kn,\qquad \gg = \frac{c}{1-c}, \end{equation} and let $\Ws$ be the sticky Walsh process as constructed above with these parameters. Then the generator $A^s$ of $\Ws$ is $1/2$ times the second derivative on $\cG$ with domain consisting of those $f\in\Cii$ which satisfy condition~\eqref{eq1.1b}.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: With $w_k=b_k/(1-c)$ and $\gg=c/(1-c)$ the sticky Walsh process realizes the boundary condition with $a=0$.
assumptions: Consider the boundary condition~\eqref{eq1.1} with $a=0$, $c\in(0,1)$, and $b\in [0,1]^n$. Set \begin{equation} w_k = \frac{b_k}{1-c},\,\kn,\qquad \gg = \frac{c}{1-c}, \end{equation} and let $\Ws$ be the sticky Walsh process as constructed above with these parameters.
conclusions: Then the generator $A^s$ of $\Ws$ is $1/2$ times the second derivative on $\cG$ with domain consisting of those $f\in\Cii$ which satisfy condition~\eqref{eq1.1b}.

nodes.name: Generator of the general Brownian motion on a star graph
nodes.statement: Consider the boundary condition~\eqref{eq1.1}, and assume that $b$ is not the null vector. Set $r=a+c\in(0,1)$, and \begin{equation} w_k = \frac{b_k}{1-r},\,\kn,\quad \gb = \frac{a}{1-r},\quad \gg = \frac{c}{1-r}. \end{equation} Let $\Wg$ be the Brownian motion as constructed above with these parameters. Then the generator $A^g$ of $\Wg$ is $1/2$ times the Laplace operator on $\cG$ with domain $\cD(A^g)$ consisting of those $f\in\Cii$ which satisfy condition~\eqref{eq1.1b}.
nodes.section: 5 The General Brownian Motion on a Single Vertex Graph
nodes.statement_short: For $b\ne 0$ the killed sticky Walsh process realizes the most general Feller boundary condition.
assumptions: Consider the boundary condition~\eqref{eq1.1}, and assume that $b$ is not the null vector. Set $r=a+c\in(0,1)$, and \begin{equation} w_k = \frac{b_k}{1-r},\,\kn,\quad \gb = \frac{a}{1-r},\quad \gg = \frac{c}{1-r}. \end{equation} Let $\Wg$ be the Brownian motion as constructed above with these parameters.

nodes.name: Boundary regularity of functions in $C_0^2(\cG)$
nodes.statement: Suppose that $f\in\Cii$, $k\in\{1,\dotsc,n\}$. Then the limit of $f'(\xi)$ as $\xi$ converges to $v$ along the open edge $l_k^\circ$ exists. The directional derivatives $f^{(i)}(v_k)$, $i=1$, $2$, of first and second order of $f$ at the vertex $v$ in direction of the edge $l_k$ exist, and the equalities \begin{equation*} f^{(i)}(v_k) = \lim_{\xi\to v,\,\xi\in l_k^\circ} f^{(i)}(\xi),\qquad i=1,\,2, \end{equation*} hold true. Moreover, $f'$ vanishes at infinity.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
nodes.statement_short: Directional derivatives of $f\in\Cii$ at the vertex exist as limits along each edge, and $f'$ vanishes at infinity.
conclusions: Then the limit of $f'(\xi)$ as $\xi$ converges to $v$ along the open edge $l_k^\circ$ exists. The directional derivatives $f^{(i)}(v_k)$, $i=1$, $2$, of first and second order of $f$ at the vertex $v$ in direction of the edge $l_k$ exist, and the equalities \begin{equation*} f^{(i)}(v_k) = \lim_{\xi\to v,\,\xi\in l_k^\circ} f^{(i)}(\xi),\qquad i=1,\,2, \end{equation*} hold true. Moreover, $f'$ vanishes at infinity.

nodes.name: Joint law of $|B_t|$ and $L_t$
nodes.statement: The joint law of $|B_t|$ and $L_t$, $t>0$, under $Q_0$ is given by \begin{equation} Q_0\bigl(|B_t|\in dx,\,L^B_t\in dy\bigr) = 2\,\frac{x+y}{\sqrt{2\pi t^3}}\,e^{-(x+y)^2/2t}\,dx\,dy,\qquad x,y\ge 0. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 1.2 Standard Brownian Motion on the Real Line
nodes.statement_short: Explicit joint density $2(x+y)(2\pi t^3)^{-1/2}e^{-(x+y)^2/2t}$ of modulus and local time.
conclusions: The joint law of $|B_t|$ and $L_t$, $t>0$, under $Q_0$ is given by \begin{equation} Q_0\bigl(|B_t|\in dx,\,L^B_t\in dy\bigr) = 2\,\frac{x+y}{\sqrt{2\pi t^3}}\,e^{-(x+y)^2/2t}\,dx\,dy,\qquad x,y\ge 0. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Law of the inverse local time $K^B_r$
nodes.statement: For any $r\ge 0$ \begin{equation} Q_0\bigl(K^B_r\in dt\bigr) = \frac{r}{t}\,g(t,r)\,dt,\qquad t>0, \end{equation} and \begin{equation} E^Q_0\bigl(e^{-\gl K^B_r}\bigr) = e^{-\sgl r},\qquad \gl>0 \end{equation} holds.
nodes.section: 1.2 Standard Brownian Motion on the Real Line
nodes.statement_short: $K^B_r$ has the stable-$1/2$ density $\frac{r}{t}g(t,r)$ and Laplace transform $e^{-\sqrt{2\gl}\,r}$.
nodes.origin_citation: Kostrykin, Potthoff & Schrader, arXiv:1008.3761, Appendix B
conclusions: \begin{equation} Q_0\bigl(K^B_r\in dt\bigr) = \frac{r}{t}\,g(t,r)\,dt,\qquad t>0, \end{equation} and \begin{equation} E^Q_0\bigl(e^{-\gl K^B_r}\bigr) = e^{-\sgl r},\qquad \gl>0 \end{equation} holds.

nodes.name: Local time at a symmetric exit time is exponential
nodes.statement: Under $Q_0$, $L^B\bigl(H^B_{\{-x,+x\}}\bigr)$, $x>0$, is exponentially distributed with mean~$x$.

nodes.name: First passage time formula for a Brownian motion on $\cG$
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a Brownian motion on $\cG$ with resolvent $R=(R_\gl,\,\gl>0)$. Then for all $\gl>0$, $\xi\in\cG$, $f\in B(\cG)$, \begin{equation} R_\gl f(\xi) = R^D_\gl f(\xi) + e_\gl(\xi)\,R_\gl f(v) \end{equation} holds true.
nodes.section: 1.3 First Passage Time Formula for Single Vertex Graphs
nodes.statement_short: The resolvent splits as the Dirichlet resolvent plus $e_\gl(\xi)R_\gl f(v)$.
assumptions: Let $X$ be a Brownian motion on $\cG$ with resolvent $R=(R_\gl,\,\gl>0)$.
conclusions: Then for all $\gl>0$, $\xi\in\cG$, $f\in B(\cG)$, \begin{equation} R_\gl f(\xi) = R^D_\gl f(\xi) + e_\gl(\xi)\,R_\gl f(v) \end{equation} holds true.

nodes.name: Resolvent of a process killed on the scale of its local time
nodes.statement: For all $\gl>0$, $f\in B(\cG)$, $\xi\in\cG$, \begin{equation} \hR_\gl f(\xi) = R_\gl f(\xi) - e_\gl(\xi)\,\hE_v\bigl(e^{-\gl \zeta_\gb}\bigr)\,R_\gl f(v) \end{equation} holds true, where $e_\gl$ is defined in equation~\eqref{eq1.14}.
nodes.section: 1.5 Killing via the Local Time at the Vertex
nodes.statement_short: $\hR_\gl f = R_\gl f - e_\gl\,\hE_v(e^{-\gl\zeta_\gb})\,R_\gl f(v)$.
conclusions: \begin{equation} \hR_\gl f(\xi) = R_\gl f(\xi) - e_\gl(\xi)\,\hE_v\bigl(e^{-\gl \zeta_\gb}\bigr)\,R_\gl f(v) \end{equation} holds true, where $e_\gl$ is defined in equation~\eqref{eq1.14}.

nodes.name: Resolvent of the Walsh process
nodes.statement: The resolvent of the Walsh process on $\cG$ is given by \begin{subequations} \begin{equation} \RW_\gl f(\xi) = \int_\cG \rW_\gl(\xi,\eta) f(\eta)\,d\eta,\qquad \gl>0,\,\xi\in\cG,\,f\in B(\cG), \end{equation} with \begin{align} \rW_\gl(\xi,\eta) &= r_\gl(\xi,\eta) + \sum_{k,m=1}^n e_{\gl,k}(\xi) \,\SW_{km} \,\frac{1}{\sgl}\,e_{\gl,m}(\eta), \\ \SW_{km} &= 2 w_m - \gd_{km}, \end{align} where $r_\gl$ is defined in equation~\eqref{eq1.22a}, and where $e_{\gl,k}$, $e_{\gl,m}$ denote the restrictions of $e_\gl$ (cf.~\eqref{eq1.14}) to the edges $l_k$, $l_m$ respectively. \end{subequations}
nodes.section: 2 The Walsh Process
nodes.statement_short: Resolvent kernel is $r_\gl$ plus a rank-structured term carrying the scattering matrix $S^w_{km}=2w_m-\gd_{km}$.
conclusions: The resolvent of the Walsh process on $\cG$ is given by \begin{subequations} \begin{equation} \RW_\gl f(\xi) = \int_\cG \rW_\gl(\xi,\eta) f(\eta)\,d\eta,\qquad \gl>0,\,\xi\in\cG,\,f\in B(\cG), \end{equation} with \begin{align} \rW_\gl(\xi,\eta) &= r_\gl(\xi,\eta) + \sum_{k,m=1}^n e_{\gl,k}(\xi) \,\SW_{km} \,\frac{1}{\sgl}\,e_{\gl,m}(\eta), \\ \SW_{km} &= 2 w_m - \gd_{km}, \end{align} where $r_\gl$ is defined in equation~\eqref{eq1.22a}, and where $e_{\gl,k}$, $e_{\gl,m}$ denote the restrictions of $e_\gl$ (cf.~\eqref{eq1.14}) to the edges $l_k$, $l_m$ respectively. \end{subequations}

nodes.name: Transition density of the Walsh process
nodes.statement: For $t>0$, $\xi$, $\eta\in\cG$ the transition density of the Walsh process on $\cG$ is given by \begin{align} \pW(t,\xi,\eta) &= p^D(t,\xi,\eta) + \sum_{k,m=1}^n \onel(\xi)\, 2w_m\, g\bigl(t,d_v(\xi,\eta)\bigr)\,\onel[m](\eta), \\ &= p(t,\xi,\eta) + \sum_{k,m=1}^n \onel(\xi)\, \SW_{km} g\bigl(t,d_v(\xi,\eta)\bigr)\,\onel[m](\eta). \end{align} $p(t,\xi,\eta)$ is defined in equation~\eqref{eq1.16}, $p^D(t,\xi,\eta)$ in equation~\eqref{eq1.20}, $g$ is the Gau{\ss}-kernel~\eqref{eq1.4}, and $d_v$ is defined in equation~\eqref{eq1.15}.
nodes.section: 2 The Walsh Process
nodes.statement_short: Dirichlet heat kernel plus $2w_m\,g(t,d_v(\xi,\eta))$, equivalently $p$ plus the scattering-matrix term.
conclusions: the transition density of the Walsh process on $\cG$ is given by \begin{align} \pW(t,\xi,\eta) &= p^D(t,\xi,\eta) + \sum_{k,m=1}^n \onel(\xi)\, 2w_m\, g\bigl(t,d_v(\xi,\eta)\bigr)\,\onel[m](\eta), \\ &= p(t,\xi,\eta) + \sum_{k,m=1}^n \onel(\xi)\, \SW_{km} g\bigl(t,d_v(\xi,\eta)\bigr)\,\onel[m](\eta). \end{align} $p(t,\xi,\eta)$ is defined in equation~\eqref{eq1.16}, $p^D(t,\xi,\eta)$ in equation~\eqref{eq1.20}, $g$ is the Gau{\ss}-kernel~\eqref{eq1.4}, and $d_v$ is defined in equation~\eqref{eq1.15}.

nodes.name: Probability of escaping the ball before elastic killing
nodes.statement: For all $\gep$, $\gb>0$, \begin{equation} \hP_v\bigl(\TW_{v,\gep} < \zeta_{\gb,0}\bigr) = \frac{1}{1+\gep\gb}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
conclusions: \begin{equation} \hP_v\bigl(\TW_{v,\gep} < \zeta_{\gb,0}\bigr) = \frac{1}{1+\gep\gb}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Laplace transform of the elastic lifetime
nodes.statement: For all $\gl$, $\gb>0$, \begin{equation*} \hE_v\bigl(e^{-\gl \zeta_{\gb,0}}\bigr) = \frac{\gb}{\gb + \sgl}. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.statement_short: $\hE_v(e^{-\gl\zeta_{\gb,0}}) = \gb/(\gb+\sqrt{2\gl})$.
conclusions: \begin{equation*} \hE_v\bigl(e^{-\gl \zeta_{\gb,0}}\bigr) = \frac{\gb}{\gb + \sgl}. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Resolvent kernel of the elastic Walsh process
nodes.statement: For $\gl>0$, $\xi$, $\eta\in\cG$ the resolvent kernel of the elastic Walsh process $\We$ is given by \begin{subequations} \begin{align} \reW_\gl(\xi,\eta) &= r^D_\gl(\xi,\eta) + \sum_{k,m=1}^n e_{\gl,k}(\xi)\,2w_m \,\frac{1}{\gb+\sgl}\,e_{\gl,m}(\eta) \\ &= r_\gl(\xi,\eta) + \sum_{k,m=1}^n e_{\gl,k}(\xi)\,\SeW_{km}(\gl) \,\frac{1}{\sgl}\, e_{\gl,m}(\eta), \end{align} with the scattering matrix $\SeW$ \begin{equation} \SeW_{km}(\gl) = 2\,\frac{\sgl}{\gb+\sgl}\,w_m - \gd_{km},\qquad \gl>0,\,k,m\in\sn. \end{equation} \end{subequations}
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.statement_short: Kernel with $\gl$-dependent scattering matrix $S^e_{km}(\gl)=2\frac{\sqrt{2\gl}}{\gb+\sqrt{2\gl}}w_m-\gd_{km}$.
conclusions: the resolvent kernel of the elastic Walsh process $\We$ is given by \begin{subequations} \begin{align} \reW_\gl(\xi,\eta) &= r^D_\gl(\xi,\eta) + \sum_{k,m=1}^n e_{\gl,k}(\xi)\,2w_m \,\frac{1}{\gb+\sgl}\,e_{\gl,m}(\eta) \\ &= r_\gl(\xi,\eta) + \sum_{k,m=1}^n e_{\gl,k}(\xi)\,\SeW_{km}(\gl) \,\frac{1}{\sgl}\, e_{\gl,m}(\eta), \end{align} with the scattering matrix $\SeW$ \begin{equation} \SeW_{km}(\gl) = 2\,\frac{\sgl}{\gb+\sgl}\,w_m - \gd_{km},\qquad \gl>0,\,k,m\in\sn. \end{equation} \end{subequations}

nodes.name: Transition density of the elastic Walsh process
nodes.statement: For $t>0$, $\xi$, $\eta\in\cG$, the transition density $\peW$ of the elastic Walsh process is given by \begin{equation} \peW(t,\xi,\eta) = p^D(t,\xi,\eta) + \sum_{k,m=1}^n \onel(\xi)\, 2w_m\,g_{\gb,0}\bigl(t,d_v(\xi,\eta)\bigr)\, \onel[m](\eta), \end{equation} and alternatively by \begin{equation} \begin{split} \peW(t,\xi,\eta) = p(t,\xi,\eta) + \sum_{k,m=1}^n &\onel(\xi)\,\Bigl(\int_0^t P_\xi(\TW_v\in ds)\\ &\times \Bigl(\seW_{km}*g\bigl(\cdot,d(v,\eta)\bigr)\Bigr)(t-s)\, \Bigr)\,\onel[m](\eta), \end{split} \end{equation} where $*$ denotes convolution.
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.statement_short: Dirichlet heat kernel plus $2w_m g_{\gb,0}(t,d_v(\xi,\eta))$, or a convolution with $s^e_{km}$.
conclusions: the transition density $\peW$ of the elastic Walsh process is given by \begin{equation} \peW(t,\xi,\eta) = p^D(t,\xi,\eta) + \sum_{k,m=1}^n \onel(\xi)\, 2w_m\,g_{\gb,0}\bigl(t,d_v(\xi,\eta)\bigr)\, \onel[m](\eta), \end{equation} and alternatively by \begin{equation} \begin{split} \peW(t,\xi,\eta) = p(t,\xi,\eta) + \sum_{k,m=1}^n &\onel(\xi)\,\Bigl(\int_0^t P_\xi(\TW_v\in ds)\\ &\times \Bigl(\seW_{km}*g\bigl(\cdot,d(v,\eta)\bigr)\Bigr)(t-s)\, \Bigr)\,\onel[m](\eta), \end{split} \end{equation} where $*$ denotes convolution.

nodes.name: Additivity of the time change $\tau$
nodes.statement: For all $s$, $t\ge 0$, a.s.\ the following formula holds true \begin{equation} \tau(s+t) = \tau(s) + \tau(t)\comp \theta_{\tau(s)}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
conclusions: a.s.\ the following formula holds true \begin{equation} \tau(s+t) = \tau(s) + \tau(t)\comp \theta_{\tau(s)}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Exit time of the sticky Walsh process
nodes.statement: $P_v$--a.s., the formula \begin{equation} \TsW_{v,\gep} = \TW_{v,\gep} + \gg\,L^w_{\TW_{v,\gep}} \end{equation} holds true.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: $\TsW_{v,\gep} = \TW_{v,\gep} + \gg L^w_{\TW_{v,\gep}}$ almost surely.
conclusions: \begin{equation} \TsW_{v,\gep} = \TW_{v,\gep} + \gg\,L^w_{\TW_{v,\gep}} \end{equation} holds true.

nodes.name: Second derivative at the vertex of the sticky resolvent
nodes.statement: Let $\gl>0$, $f\in \Co$. Then \begin{equation} \frac{1}{2} \bigl(\RsW_\gl f\bigr)''(v) = \frac{1}{\sgl +\gg\gl}\,\Bigl(2\gl\,(e^w_\gl,f) - \sgl f(v)\Bigr) \end{equation} holds, where \begin{equation} e^w_\gl(\xi) = w_k\,e_\gl(\xi),\qquad \xi\in l_k,\,\kn, \end{equation} and $e_\gl$ is defined in equation~\eqref{eq1.14}.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: $\tfrac12(\RsW_\gl f)''(v)$ in closed form via the weighted exponential $e^w_\gl$.
conclusions: Then \begin{equation} \frac{1}{2} \bigl(\RsW_\gl f\bigr)''(v) = \frac{1}{\sgl +\gg\gl}\,\Bigl(2\gl\,(e^w_\gl,f) - \sgl f(v)\Bigr) \end{equation} holds, where \begin{equation} e^w_\gl(\xi) = w_k\,e_\gl(\xi),\qquad \xi\in l_k,\,\kn, \end{equation} and $e_\gl$ is defined in equation~\eqref{eq1.14}.

nodes.name: Inverse local times of the sticky and Walsh processes
nodes.statement: For all $\gg\ge 0$, the following relation holds true: \begin{equation} K^s_r = K^w_r + \gg r,\qquad r\in\R_+. \end{equation}

nodes.statement_short: $K^s_r = K^w_r + \gg r$.
conclusions: the following relation holds true: \begin{equation} K^s_r = K^w_r + \gg r,\qquad r\in\R_+. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Derivative of the resolvent at the vertex
nodes.statement: For every Brownian motion $X$ on $\cG$ with resolvent $R=(R_\gl,\,\gl>0)$, and all $f\in\Co$, \begin{equation} (R_\gl f)'(v_k) = 2(e_{\gl,k},f_k) - \sgl R_\gl f(v),\qquad k\in\sn, \end{equation} holds true.

nodes.statement_short: $(R_\gl f)'(v_k)=2(e_{\gl,k},f_k)-\sqrt{2\gl}R_\gl f(v)$ for every Brownian motion on $\cG$.
assumptions: For every Brownian motion $X$ on $\cG$ with resolvent $R=(R_\gl,\,\gl>0)$, and all $f\in\Co$,

nodes.statement: For every $\gg\ge 0$, \begin{equation} E_v\bigl(\TsW_{v,\gep}\bigr)=\gep^2+\gg\gep \end{equation} holds.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: $E_v(\TsW_{v,\gep})=\gep^2+\gg\gep$.
conclusions: \begin{equation} E_v\bigl(\TsW_{v,\gep}\bigr)=\gep^2+\gg\gep \end{equation} holds.

nodes.name: Value at the vertex of the sticky resolvent
nodes.statement: Let $\gl>0$, and $f\in\Co$. Then \begin{equation} \RsW_\gl f(v) = \frac{1}{\sgl+\gg\gl}\,\bigl(2\,(e^w_\gl,f)+\gg f(v)\bigr) \end{equation} holds.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
conclusions: Then \begin{equation} \RsW_\gl f(v) = \frac{1}{\sgl+\gg\gl}\,\bigl(2\,(e^w_\gl,f)+\gg f(v)\bigr) \end{equation} holds.

nodes.name: Resolvent kernel of the Walsh process with sticky vertex
nodes.statement: For $\xi$, $\eta\in\cG$, $\gl>0$, the resolvent kernel $\rsW_\gl$, of the Walsh process with sticky vertex is given by \begin{equation} \begin{split} \rsW_\gl(\xi,d\eta) = r^D_\gl(\xi,\eta)\,d\eta +\sum_{k,m=1}^n e_{\gl,k}(\xi)\,\,&2w_m\,\frac{1}{\sgl+\gg\gl}\,e_{\gl,m}(\eta)\,d\eta\\ &\quad + \frac{\gg}{\sgl +\gg\gl}\,e_\gl(\xi)\,\epsilon_v(d\eta), \end{split} \end{equation} with $r^D_\gl$ defined in~\eqref{eq1.22}, and $\epsilon_v$ denotes the Dirac measure in $v$. Alternatively, $\rsW_\gl$ is given by \begin{subequations} \begin{equation} \begin{split} \rsW_\gl(\xi,d\eta) = r_\gl(\xi,\eta)\,d\eta +\sum_{k,m=1}^n e_{\gl,k}(\xi)\,&\SsW_{km}(\gl)\,\frac{1}{\sgl}\,e_{\gl,m}(\eta)\,d\eta\\ &\quad + \frac{\gg}{\sgl +\gg\gl}\,e_\gl(\xi)\,\epsilon_v(d\eta), \end{split} \end{equation} where $r_\gl$ is defined in equation~\eqref{eq1.22a}, and \begin{equation} \SsW_{km}(\gl) = 2\,\frac{\sgl}{\sgl+\gg\gl}\,w_m - \gd_{km}. \end{equation} \end{subequations}
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Kernel has an extra atom $\frac{\gg}{\sqrt{2\gl}+\gg\gl}e_\gl(\xi)\epsilon_v(d\eta)$ at the vertex.
conclusions: the resolvent kernel $\rsW_\gl$, of the Walsh process with sticky vertex is given by \begin{equation} \begin{split} \rsW_\gl(\xi,d\eta) = r^D_\gl(\xi,\eta)\,d\eta +\sum_{k,m=1}^n e_{\gl,k}(\xi)\,\,&2w_m\,\frac{1}{\sgl+\gg\gl}\,e_{\gl,m}(\eta)\,d\eta\\ &\quad + \frac{\gg}{\sgl +\gg\gl}\,e_\gl(\xi)\,\epsilon_v(d\eta), \end{split} \end{equation} with $r^D_\gl$ defined in~\eqref{eq1.22}, and $\epsilon_v$ denotes the Dirac measure in $v$. Alternatively, $\rsW_\gl$ is given by \begin{subequations} \begin{equation} \begin{split} \rsW_\gl(\xi,d\eta) = r_\gl(\xi,\eta)\,d\eta +\sum_{k,m=1}^n e_{\gl,k}(\xi)\,&\SsW_{km}(\gl)\,\frac{1}{\sgl}\,e_{\gl,m}(\eta)\,d\eta\\ &\quad + \frac{\gg}{\sgl +\gg\gl}\,e_\gl(\xi)\,\epsilon_v(d\eta), \end{split} \end{equation} where $r_\gl$ is defined in equation~\eqref{eq1.22a}, and \begin{equation} \SsW_{km}(\gl) = 2\,\frac{\sgl}{\sgl+\gg\gl}\,w_m - \gd_{km}. \end{equation} \end{subequations}

nodes.name: Transition kernel of the Walsh process with sticky vertex
nodes.statement: For $t>0$, $\xi$, $\eta\in\cG$ the transition kernel of the Walsh process with sticky vertex is given by \begin{equation} \begin{split} \psW(t,\xi,\eta) &= p^D(t,\xi,\eta)\,d\eta\\[1ex] &\qquad + \sum_{k,m=1}^n \onel(\xi)\,2w_m \,g_{0,\gg}\bigl(t,d_v(\xi,\eta)\bigr)\onel[m](\eta)\,d\eta\\[1ex] &\qquad + \gg\,g_{0,\gg}\bigl(t, d(\xi,v)\bigr)\,\epsilon_v(d\eta) \end{split} \end{equation} where $p^D$ is defined in equation~\eqref{eq1.20}, or alternatively by \begin{equation} \begin{split} \psW(t,\xi,d\eta) &= p(t,\xi,\eta)\,d\eta\\ &\qquad +\sum_{k,m=1}^n \onel(\xi)\,\Bigl( 2w_m\,g_{0,\gg}\bigl(t,d_v(\xi,\eta)\bigr)\,d\eta\\[-1ex] &\hspace{9.5em} -\gd_{km}\,g\bigl(t,d_v(\xi,\eta)\bigr)\,d\eta\Bigr)\, \onel[m](\eta)\\[1ex] &\qquad +\gg\,g_{0,\gg}\bigl(t, d(\xi,v)\bigr)\,\epsilon_v(d\eta), \end{split} \end{equation} and $p(t,a,b)$ is given in formula~\eqref{eq1.16}.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Dirichlet part plus $2w_m g_{0,\gg}$ plus a Dirac mass $\gg g_{0,\gg}(t,d(\xi,v))$ at the vertex.
conclusions: the transition kernel of the Walsh process with sticky vertex is given by \begin{equation} \begin{split} \psW(t,\xi,\eta) &= p^D(t,\xi,\eta)\,d\eta\\[1ex] &\qquad + \sum_{k,m=1}^n \onel(\xi)\,2w_m \,g_{0,\gg}\bigl(t,d_v(\xi,\eta)\bigr)\onel[m](\eta)\,d\eta\\[1ex] &\qquad + \gg\,g_{0,\gg}\bigl(t, d(\xi,v)\bigr)\,\epsilon_v(d\eta) \end{split} \end{equation} where $p^D$ is defined in equation~\eqref{eq1.20}, or alternatively by \begin{equation} \begin{split} \psW(t,\xi,d\eta) &= p(t,\xi,\eta)\,d\eta\\ &\qquad +\sum_{k,m=1}^n \onel(\xi)\,\Bigl( 2w_m\,g_{0,\gg}\bigl(t,d_v(\xi,\eta)\bigr)\,d\eta\\[-1ex] &\hspace{9.5em} -\gd_{km}\,g\bigl(t,d_v(\xi,\eta)\bigr)\,d\eta\Bigr)\, \onel[m](\eta)\\[1ex] &\qquad +\gg\,g_{0,\gg}\bigl(t, d(\xi,v)\bigr)\,\epsilon_v(d\eta), \end{split} \end{equation} and $p(t,a,b)$ is given in formula~\eqref{eq1.16}.

nodes.name: Density and Laplace transform of $K^s_r$
nodes.statement: For $r\ge 0$, $K^s_r$ has the density \begin{equation} P_v(K^s_r\in dl) = \frac{r}{\sqrt{2\pi (l-\gg r)^3}}\,e^{-r^2/2(l-\gg r)}\,dl,\qquad l\ge \gg r. \end{equation} Furthermore, the Laplace transform of the density of $K^s_r$ under $P_v$ is given by \begin{equation} E_v\bigl(e^{-\gl K^s_r}\bigr) = e^{-(\sgl + \gl \gg)r},\qquad \gl >0. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 5 The General Brownian Motion on a Single Vertex Graph
nodes.statement_short: $K^s_r$ is the stable-$1/2$ variable shifted by $\gg r$; its Laplace transform is $e^{-(\sqrt{2\gl}+\gl\gg)r}$.
conclusions: $K^s_r$ has the density \begin{equation} P_v(K^s_r\in dl) = \frac{r}{\sqrt{2\pi (l-\gg r)^3}}\,e^{-r^2/2(l-\gg r)}\,dl,\qquad l\ge \gg r. \end{equation} Furthermore, the Laplace transform of the density of $K^s_r$ under $P_v$ is given by \begin{equation} E_v\bigl(e^{-\gl K^s_r}\bigr) = e^{-(\sgl + \gl \gg)r},\qquad \gl >0. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Decomposition of the general lifetime
nodes.statement: For all $\gb>0$, $\gg\ge0$, the following equation holds true \begin{equation} \zeta_{\gb,\gg} = \zeta_{\gb,0}+\gg S. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 5 The General Brownian Motion on a Single Vertex Graph
nodes.statement_short: $\zeta_{\gb,\gg} = \zeta_{\gb,0}+\gg S$.
conclusions: the following equation holds true \begin{equation} \zeta_{\gb,\gg} = \zeta_{\gb,0}+\gg S. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Laplace transform of the general lifetime
nodes.statement: For all $\gb>0$, $\gg\ge 0$, $\gl>0$, the following formula holds true \begin{subequations} \begin{equation} \hE_v\bigl(e^{-\gl \zeta_{\gb,\gg}}\bigr) = \gb \rho(\gl), \end{equation} with \begin{equation} \rho(\gl) = \frac{1}{\gb+\sgl+\gg\gl}. \end{equation} \end{subequations}
nodes.section: 5 The General Brownian Motion on a Single Vertex Graph
nodes.statement_short: $\hE_v(e^{-\gl\zeta_{\gb,\gg}}) = \gb/(\gb+\sqrt{2\gl}+\gg\gl)$.
conclusions: the following formula holds true \begin{subequations} \begin{equation} \hE_v\bigl(e^{-\gl \zeta_{\gb,\gg}}\bigr) = \gb \rho(\gl), \end{equation} with \begin{equation} \rho(\gl) = \frac{1}{\gb+\sgl+\gg\gl}. \end{equation} \end{subequations}

nodes.name: Resolvent of the general Brownian motion
nodes.statement: For all $f\in\Co$, $\gl>0$, $\xi\in\cG$ the following formula holds true: \begin{equation} \Rg_\gl f(\xi) = \RsW_\gl f(\xi) - \gb\rho(\gl)\,e_\gl(\xi)\,\RsW_\gl f(v). \end{equation}

nodes.statement_short: $\Rg_\gl f = \RsW_\gl f - \gb\rho(\gl)e_\gl\RsW_\gl f(v)$.
conclusions: the following formula holds true: \begin{equation} \Rg_\gl f(\xi) = \RsW_\gl f(\xi) - \gb\rho(\gl)\,e_\gl(\xi)\,\RsW_\gl f(v). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Resolvent kernel of the general Brownian motion
nodes.statement: For $\xi$, $\eta\in\cG$, $\gl>0$, the resolvent kernel $\rg_\gl$ of the general Brownian motion $\Wg$ on $\cG$ is given by \begin{equation} \begin{split} \rg_\gl(\xi,d\eta) = r^D_\gl(\xi,\eta)\,d\eta +\sum_{k,m=1}^n e_{\gl,k}&(\xi)\,2w_m\,\rho(\gl)\,e_{\gl,m}(\eta)\,d\eta\\ & + \gg\,\rho(\gl)\,e_\gl(\xi)\,\epsilon_v(d\eta), \end{split} \end{equation} with $r^D_\gl$ as in formula~\eqref{eq1.22}, and $\rho$ is defined in equation~\eqref{eq5.3b}. Alternatively, $\rg_\gl$ can be written in the following form \begin{subequations} \begin{equation} \begin{split} \rg_\gl(\xi,d\eta) = r_\gl(\xi,\eta)\,d\eta +\sum_{k,m=1}^n e_{\gl,k}&(\xi)\,\Sg_{km}(\gl) \,\frac{1}{\sgl}\,e_{\gl,m}(\eta)\,d\eta\\ & + \gg\,\rho(\gl)\,e_\gl(\xi)\,\epsilon_v(d\eta), \end{split} \end{equation} where $r_\gl$ is defined in equation~\eqref{eq1.22a}, and \begin{equation} \Sg_{km}(\gl) = 2\,\sgl\,\rho(\gl)\,w_m - \gd_{km}. \end{equation} \end{subequations}
nodes.section: 5 The General Brownian Motion on a Single Vertex Graph
nodes.statement_short: Dirichlet kernel plus $2w_m\rho(\gl)$ term plus a vertex atom; scattering matrix $S^g_{km}(\gl)=2\sqrt{2\gl}\rho(\gl)w_m-\gd_{km}$.
conclusions: the resolvent kernel $\rg_\gl$ of the general Brownian motion $\Wg$ on $\cG$ is given by \begin{equation} \begin{split} \rg_\gl(\xi,d\eta) = r^D_\gl(\xi,\eta)\,d\eta +\sum_{k,m=1}^n e_{\gl,k}&(\xi)\,2w_m\,\rho(\gl)\,e_{\gl,m}(\eta)\,d\eta\\ & + \gg\,\rho(\gl)\,e_\gl(\xi)\,\epsilon_v(d\eta), \end{split} \end{equation} with $r^D_\gl$ as in formula~\eqref{eq1.22}, and $\rho$ is defined in equation~\eqref{eq5.3b}. Alternatively, $\rg_\gl$ can be written in the following form \begin{subequations} \begin{equation} \begin{split} \rg_\gl(\xi,d\eta) = r_\gl(\xi,\eta)\,d\eta +\sum_{k,m=1}^n e_{\gl,k}&(\xi)\,\Sg_{km}(\gl) \,\frac{1}{\sgl}\,e_{\gl,m}(\eta)\,d\eta\\ & + \gg\,\rho(\gl)\,e_\gl(\xi)\,\epsilon_v(d\eta), \end{split} \end{equation} where $r_\gl$ is defined in equation~\eqref{eq1.22a}, and \begin{equation} \Sg_{km}(\gl) = 2\,\sgl\,\rho(\gl)\,w_m - \gd_{km}. \end{equation} \end{subequations}

nodes.name: Transition kernel of the general Brownian motion
nodes.statement: For $\xi$, $\eta\in\cG$, $t>0$, the transition kernel of the general Brownian motion $\Wg$ on $\cG$ is given by \begin{equation} \begin{split} \pg(t,\xi,d\eta) &= p^D(t,\xi,\eta)\,d\eta\\ &\hspace{2em} +\sum_{k,m=1}^n \onel(\xi)\,2w_m\,g_{\gb,\gg}\bigl(t,d_v(\xi,\eta)\bigr)\, \onel[m](\eta)\,d\eta\\ &\hspace{2em} + \gg\,g_{\gb,\gg}\bigl(t,d(\xi,v)\bigr)\,\gep_v(d\eta), \end{split} \end{equation} which alternatively can be written as \begin{equation} \begin{split} \pg(t,\xi,d\eta) &= p(t,\xi,\eta)\,d\eta\\ &\hspace{2em} +\sum_{k,m=1}^n \onel(\xi)\,\Bigl(2w_m\,g_{\gb,\gg}\bigl(t,d_v(\xi,\eta)\bigr)\\ &\hspace{10em} -\gd_{km}\,g\bigl(t,d_v(\xi,\eta)\bigr)\Bigl)\, \onel[m](\eta)\,d\eta\\ &\hspace{2em} + \gg\,g_{\gb,\gg}\bigl(t,d(\xi,v)\bigr)\,\gep_v(d\eta). \end{split} \end{equation}
nodes.section: 5 The General Brownian Motion on a Single Vertex Graph
nodes.statement_short: Same shape as the sticky kernel with $g_{0,\gg}$ replaced by $g_{\gb,\gg}$.
conclusions: the transition kernel of the general Brownian motion $\Wg$ on $\cG$ is given by \begin{equation} \begin{split} \pg(t,\xi,d\eta) &= p^D(t,\xi,\eta)\,d\eta\\ &\hspace{2em} +\sum_{k,m=1}^n \onel(\xi)\,2w_m\,g_{\gb,\gg}\bigl(t,d_v(\xi,\eta)\bigr)\, \onel[m](\eta)\,d\eta\\ &\hspace{2em} + \gg\,g_{\gb,\gg}\bigl(t,d(\xi,v)\bigr)\,\gep_v(d\eta), \end{split} \end{equation} which alternatively can be written as \begin{equation} \begin{split} \pg(t,\xi,d\eta) &= p(t,\xi,\eta)\,d\eta\\ &\hspace{2em} +\sum_{k,m=1}^n \onel(\xi)\,\Bigl(2w_m\,g_{\gb,\gg}\bigl(t,d_v(\xi,\eta)\bigr)\\ &\hspace{10em} -\gd_{km}\,g\bigl(t,d_v(\xi,\eta)\bigr)\Bigl)\, \onel[m](\eta)\,d\eta\\ &\hspace{2em} + \gg\,g_{\gb,\gg}\bigl(t,d(\xi,v)\bigr)\,\gep_v(d\eta). \end{split} \end{equation}

nodes.name: Conventions on diffusion processes and filtrations
nodes.statement: By a diffusion process we mean a strong Markov process (e.g., in the sense of~\cite{BlGe68}), which a.s.\ has c\`adl\`ag paths and a.s.\ the paths are continuous on $[0,\zeta)$, where $\zeta$ is its lifetime. Moreover, in definition~\ref{def_BM} we have --- as we shall usually do without any danger of confusion --- identified the external leg $l_k$, $k=1$, \dots, $n$, on which the process starts with the corresponding copy of $\R_+$. Throughout we shall assume without loss of generality that the filtration of a Brownian motion on $\cG$ satisfies the ``usual conditions'', i.e., it is right continuous and complete relative to the underlying family $(P_\xi,\,\xi\in\cG)$ of probability measures.

nodes.name: Second derivatives at the vertex agree across edges
nodes.statement: By definition we have that for every $f\in\Cii$ and all $j$, $k=1$, \dots, $n$, $f''(v_j) = f''(v_k)$, and henceforth we shall simply write $f''(v)$ for this quantity. On the other hand, in general $f'(v_j)\ne f'(v_k)$ for $j\ne k$.

nodes.statement_short: $f''(v_j)=f''(v_k)$ for $f\in\Cii$, while first derivatives generally differ.

nodes.name: Usefulness of the killed-resolvent formula
nodes.statement: Formula~\eqref{eq1.30} is quite useful, because if the resolvent of $X$ is known, then --- in view of equation~\eqref{eq1.14} --- it reduces the calculation of $\hR_\gl$ to the computation of the Laplace transform of the density of $\zeta_\gb$ under $\hP_v$.

nodes.name: The scattering matrix of the Walsh process
nodes.statement: The matrix $\SW=\bigl(\SW_{km},\,k,m = 1,\dotsc,n\bigr)$ is the \emph{scattering matrix} as defined in quantum mechanics. We briefly recall its construction in the present context, for more details the interested reader is referred to~\cite{KoSc99}. $\SW$ is obtained from the boundary conditions at the vertex $v$ in the following way. Consider a function $f$ on $\cG$ which is continuously differentiable in $\cGo=\cG\setminus\{v\}$, and such that for all $\kn$ the limits \begin{align*} F_k &= f(v_k) = \lim_{\xi\to v,\,\xi\in l_k\op} f(\xi)\\ F'_k &= f'(v_k) = \lim_{\xi\to v,\,\xi\in l_k\op} f'(\xi) \end{align*} exist. Define two column vectors $F$, $F'\in\C^n$, having the components $F_k$ and $F'_k$, $\kn$, respectively. Furthermore, consider boundary conditions of the following form \begin{equation} A F + B F' =0, \end{equation} where $A$ and $B$ are complex $n\times n$ matrices. The \emph{on-shell scattering matrix at energy $E>0$} is defined as \begin{equation} S_{A,B}(E) = - (A+i\sqrt{E}B)^{-1}(A-i\sqrt{E}B), \end{equation} which exists and is unitary, provided the $n\times 2n$ matrix $(A,B)$ has maximal rank (i.e., rank $n$) and $AB^\dagger$ is hermitian. These requirements for $A$ and $B$ guarantee that the corresponding Laplace operator is self-adjoint on $L^2(\cG)$ (with Lebesgue measure). Observe that under these conditions the boundary conditions~\eqref{bc} are equivalent to any boundary conditions of the form $CAF+CBF'=0$ where $C$ is invertible. Also $S_{CA, CB}(E) = S_{A,B}(E)$ holds true. For the Walsh process at hand, concrete choices for $A$ and $B$ are given by \begin{equation*} A^w=\begin{pmatrix} 0&0&0&\ldots&0&0\\ 1&-1&0&\ldots&0&0\\ 0&1&-1&\ldots&0&0\\ 0&0&1&\ldots &0&0\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&1&-1 \end{pmatrix},\ B^w=\begin{pmatrix} b_1&b_2&b_3&\ldots&b_{n-1}&b_n\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&0&0\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&0&0\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&0&0\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&0&0 \end{pmatrix}. \end{equation*} Then~\eqref{bc} is the condition that $f$ is actually continuous at the vertex $v$, i.e., $f(v_k)=f(v_m)$, $k$, $m=1,\dotsc,n$, and that~\eqref{eq2.2} is valid (with $w_k=b_k$, $k\in\sn$). Obviously, $(A^w, B^w)$ has maximal rank. However, $A^w (B^w)^\dagger$ is hermitian if and only if all $b_k$ are equal (i.e., $b_k = 1/n$, $\kn$). Nevertheless, \eqref{SE} exists also in the non-hermitian case, and $S_{A^w, B^w}(E)=S^w$ holds for all $E>0$ due to the relations $A^w S^w = - A^w$, and $B^w S^w = B^w$. In addition, the following relations are valid: \begin{align} \SW &= \bigl(\SW\bigr)^{-1}, \\ \det \SW &= (-1)^{n+1}. \end{align} Furthermore, $S^w$ is a contraction, and the associated Laplace operator is m-dissipative on $L^2(\cG)$ since trivially $\text{Im}(AB^\dagger)=0$, cf.\ Theorem~2.5 in~\cite{KoPo09c}. When all $b_k$ are equal, such that $A^w(B^w)^\dag=0$, then $S^w$ is an involutive, orthogonal matrix of the form \begin{equation} S^w = - \1 + 2P_n. \end{equation} $P_n$ is the matrix whose entries are equal to $1/n$. $P_n$ is a real orthogonal projection, that is $P_n = P_n^\dag = P_n^t = P_n^2$. It is also of rank $1$, that is $\dim \text{Ran} P_n = 1$. The relation~\eqref{eq2.4b} giving the resolvent in terms of the scattering matrix is actually valid in the more general context of arbitrary metric graphs and boundary conditions of the form~\eqref{bc}, see~\cite{KoSc06, KoPo09c}.
nodes.section: 2 The Walsh Process
nodes.statement_short: Derives $S^w$ from vertex boundary conditions $A^wF+B^wF'=0$ and records $S^w=(S^w)^{-1}$, $\det S^w=(-1)^{n+1}$.

nodes.name: Alternative form of the Walsh transition density
nodes.statement: Alternatively $\pW(t,\xi,\eta)$ can also be written as \begin{equation} \begin{split} \pW(t,\xi,\eta) &= p(t,\xi,\eta)\\ &\ + \sum_{k,m=1}^n \onel(\xi) \int_0^t P_\xi(H_v\in ds)\, \SW_{km}\, g\bigl(t-s,d(v,\eta)\bigr)\,\onel[m](\eta). \end{split} \end{equation} Even though this formula appears somewhat more complicated than~\eqref{eq2.8}, it exhibits the role of the scattering matrix $\SW$, that is, it describes more clearly what happens when the process hits the vertex.

nodes.name: Consistency of the elastic parameters
nodes.statement: Note that condition~\eqref{eq1.1a} entails that if $w_k$ and $\gb$ are defined by~\eqref{eq3.4} then $w_k\in [0,1]$, $\kn$, $\sum_k w_k=1$, and $\gb>0$. Therefore the choice~\eqref{eq3.4} is consistent with the conditions on these parameters required by the construction of the elastic Walsh process $\We$.
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process

nodes.name: Energy dependence of the elastic scattering matrix
nodes.statement: Note that in contrast to the case of the Walsh process, this time the scattering matrix is not constant with respect to $\gl>0$. Also, when $\gb=0$, formula~\eqref{eq2.4c} is recovered, as it should be. In analogy with the discussion in remark~\ref{rem2.4}, the boundary conditions for the elastic Walsh process is given by the matrices \begin{equation*} A^e = \begin{pmatrix} 0&0&0&\ldots&0&\gb\\ 1&-1&0&\ldots&0&0\\ 0&1&-1&\ldots&0&0\\ 0&0&1&\ldots &0&0\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&1&-1 \end{pmatrix},\ B^e=\begin{pmatrix} w_1&w_2&w_3&\ldots&w_{n-1}&w_n\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&0&0\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&0&0\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&0&0\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&0&0 \end{pmatrix}, \end{equation*} such that \begin{align*} \SeW(\gl) &= S_{A^e,B^e}(E=-2\gl)\\ &= - (A^e+\sgl B^e)^{-1}\,(A^e-\sgl B^e). \end{align*} Observe that for $k$, $m\in\{1,\dotsc,n\}$ the matrix element $\SeW_{km}(\gl)$ of the scattering matrix is obtained from the resolvent kernel as \begin{equation*} \SeW_{km}(\gl) = \sgl\,\lim_{\xi,\,\eta\to v}\bigl(\reW_\gl(\xi,\eta) - r_\gl(\xi,\eta)\bigr), \end{equation*} where the limit on the right hand side is taken in such a way that $\xi$, $\eta$ converge to $v$ along the edges $l_k$, $l_m$ respectively. $\SeW_{km}(\gl)$ in turn fixes the data $w_m$ and $\gb$, e.g., via the behavior for large $\gl$, that is from the behavior at ``large energies'' \begin{equation*} w_m = \frac{1}{2}\bigl(\gd_{km} + \lim_{\gl'\ua\infty} \SeW_{km}(\gl')\bigr), \quad \text{for all $k\in\sn$}, \end{equation*} and \begin{equation*} \gb = \sgl\Bigl(\frac{\gd_{km}+\lim_{\gl'\ua\infty}\SeW_{km}(\gl')} {\gd_{km}+\SeW_{mm}(\gl)}-1\Bigr),\quad \text{for all $\gl$, and all $k$, $m\in\sn$}. \end{equation*} Alternatively, the data can be obtained from the small $\gl$ behavior, that is the threshold behavior, of the scattering matrix, since from \begin{equation*} \frac{w_m}{\gb} = \lim_{\gl \da 0} \frac{1}{2\sgl}\bigl(\SeW_{km}(\gl)+\gd_{km}\bigr) \qquad \text{for all $k\in\sn$}, \end{equation*} we obtain \begin{equation*} \gb^{-1} = \frac{1}{2\sgl}\Bigl(\sum_{m=1}^n\SeW_{km}(\gl)+1\Bigr) \qquad \text{for all $k\in\sn$}, \end{equation*} and therefore \begin{equation*} w_m = \frac{\lim_{\gl\da 0} \gl^{-1/2}\bigl(\SeW_{km}(\gl)+\gd_{km}\bigr)} {\lim_{\gl\da 0} \gl^{-1/2}\Bigl(\sum_m\SeW_{k'm}(\gl)+1\Bigr)} \qquad \text{for all $k$, $k'\in\sn$}. \end{equation*} Furthermore we remark that in the context of quantum mechanics in the self-adjoint case $w_k=1/n$, $\kn$, the boundary conditions of the elastic Walsh process are interpreted as the presence of a $\gd$--potential of strength $\gb$ at the vertex.
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.statement_short: $S^e(\gl)$ is $\gl$-dependent; the data $w_m,\gb$ are recoverable from its high- and low-energy behaviour.

nodes.name: Quantum interpretation of the sticky vertex
nodes.statement: When all $w_m$, $m=1$, \dots, $n$, are equal to $1/n$, the matrix $S^s(\gl)$ takes the form \begin{equation*} S^s(\gl) = -\1 + \frac{2\sgl}{\sgl + \gg \gl}\,P_n \end{equation*} which reduces to~\eqref{eq2.6a} when $\gg=0$. $S^s(\gl)$ is unitary for all $\gl<0$. Also the $S^s(\gl)$ for different $\gl$ all commute. As a consequence $S^s(\gl)$ has the interpretation of a quantum scattering matrix in the sense of~\cite{KoSc99}. More precisely, $S^s(\gl)$ stems from the Schr\"odinger operator $-\gD^s$, where $\gD^s$ is a self-adjoint Laplace operator on $L^2(\cG)$ with boundary conditions of the form~\eqref{bc} with the choice \begin{equation} \begin{split} A &= - \frac{1}{2}\,\bigl(S^s(\gl_0)+\1\bigr),\\ B &= - \frac{1}{2\sqrt{\mathstrut2\gl_0}}\,\bigl(S^s(\gl_0)-\1\bigr), \end{split} \end{equation} for any $\gl_0$ for which $\sqrt{2\gl_0}+\gg\gl_0\ne 0$. We emphasize that the Schr\"odinger operator $-\gD^s$ and the generator $A^s$ of the Walsh process are quite different: Not only do they act on different Banach spaces, but also the functions in the intersection of their domains satisfy different boundary conditions at the vertex $v$. As matter of fact, the integral kernel of the resolvent $(-\gD^s+2\gl)^{-1}$ of the Schr\"odinger operator $-\gD^s$ is given by, see Lemma~4.2 in~\cite{KoSc06}, \begin{equation*} \frac{1}{2}\Bigl(r_\gl(\xi,\eta) +\sum_{k,m=1}^n e_{\gl,k}(\xi)\, \SsW_{km}(\gl)\,\frac{1}{\sgl}\,e_{\gl,m}(\eta)\Bigl), \end{equation*} that is --- up to a factor $2$ --- by the right hand side of~\eqref{eq4.14a} \emph{without} the last term. In more detail and with the definition~\eqref{SE} \begin{equation*} S_{A,B}\bigl(E=-2\gl\bigr) = S^s(\gl) \end{equation*} holds for all $\gl>0$. As a function of $k$ ($k^2=E$), $S^s$ is meromorphic in the complex $k$--plane with a pole on the positive imaginary axis at $k^b=2i/\gg$. This corresponds to a negative eigenvalue $E^b=-4/\gg^2$ of $-\gD^s$. The corresponding (normalized) eigenfunction $\psi^b$ --- physically speaking a \emph{bound state} --- is given as \begin{equation*} \psi^b(\xi) = \frac{1}{2}\,\sqrt{\frac{\gg}{n}}\,e^{-2 d(v,\xi)/\gg},\qquad \xi\in\cG. \end{equation*} So quantum mechanically the vertex $v$ acts like an attractive potential. We view this as a quantum analogue of the stickiness of the vertex $v$. This analogy can be elaborated a bit further by inspecting the associated quantum mechanical time delay matrix (see, e.g., \cite{AmJa77, BrFr02, JaMi72, Ma76, Ma81, Na80, Wi55}) \begin{equation*} T(k) = \frac{1}{2ik}\,S(k)^{-1}\frac{\p}{\p k} S(k) \end{equation*} which in the present context gives \begin{equation*} T(k) = \frac{-2\gg}{k(4+k^2\gg^2)}\,P_n. \end{equation*} So $T(k)$ has zero as an $(n-1)$--fold eigenvalue plus the non-degenerate eigenvalue \begin{equation*} \frac{-2\gg}{k(4+k^2\gg^2)}, \end{equation*} which for $\gg>0$ is the signal for a strict quantum delay. Observe that for $k\to +\infty$, that is for large energies, the time delay experienced by the quantum particle tends to zero, while for $k\to 0$, i.e., for low energies, the delay becomes arbitrarily large. From the physical point of view, both effects are clearly to be expected. For comparison and in contrast to the present stochastic context, in quantum mechanics $\gg<0$ is also allowed for a meaningful Schr\"odinger operator and an associated scattering matrix.

nodes.name: Every Brownian motion on a star graph is a Feller process
nodes.statement: It is not hard to show that every Brownian motion on a star graph is a Feller process. A convenient way to prove this is to show that its resolvent maps $C_0(\cG)$ into itself by arguments similar to those in~\cite[Section~3.6]{ItMc74}, and to observe that the path properties imply for all $\xi\in\cG$, $f\in\Co$, $P_t f(\xi)$ converges to $f(\xi)$ as $t$ decreases to $0$, where $(P_t,\,t\in\R_+)$ denotes the semigroup generated by the Brownian motion. nodes.statement: For $\gl>0$, $f\in B(\cG)$, $\xi\in\cG$ \begin{align*} \hR_\gl f(\xi) &= \hE_\xi\Bigl(\int_0^{\zeta_\gb} e^{-\gl t} f(X_t)\,dt\Bigr)\\ &= R_\gl f(\xi) - \hE_\xi\Bigl(e^{-\gl\zeta_\gb} \int_0^\infty e^{-\gl t}\,f\bigl(X_{t+\zeta_\gb}\bigr)\,dt\Bigr). \end{align*} By construction, the last expectation value is equal to \begin{equation*} \gb\int_0^\infty e^{-\gb s}\int_0^\infty e^{-\gl t} E_\xi\Bigl(e^{-\gl K_s}\,f\bigl(X_{t+K_s}\bigr)\Bigr)\,dt\,ds, \end{equation*} where we used Fubini's theorem. Consider the expectation value under the integrals, and recall that for fixed $s\in\R_+$, $K_s$ is an $\cF$--stopping time, while $X$ is strongly Markovian relative to $\cF$. Hence we can compute as follows \begin{align*} E_\xi\Bigl(e^{-\gl K_s}\,f\bigl(X_{t+K_s}\bigr)\Bigr) &= E_\xi\Bigl(e^{-\gl K_s}\,E_\xi\Bigl(f\bigl(X_{t+K_s}\bigr)\cond \cF_{K_s}\Bigr)\Bigr)\\ &= E_\xi\Bigl(e^{-\gl K_s}\,E_{X(K_s)}\bigl(f(X_t)\bigr)\Bigr)\\ &= E_\xi\bigl(e^{-\gl K_s}\bigr)\,E_v\bigl(f(X_t)\bigr), \end{align*} where we used the fact that a.s.\ $X(K_s)=v$. So far we have established \begin{equation*} \hR_\gl f(\xi) = R_\gl f(\xi) - \hE_\xi\bigl(e^{-\gl \zeta_\gb}\bigr)\,R_\gl f(v). \end{equation*} In order to compute the expectation value on the right hand side, we first remark that because $L$ is zero until $X$ hits the vertex for the first time, we find that for given $s\in\R_+$, $K_s\ge H_v$, and therefore $K_s = H_v + K_s\comp \theta_{H_v}$. Hence, and again by the strong Markov property, \begin{align*} E_\xi\bigl(e^{-\gl K_s}\bigr) &= E_\xi\bigl(e^{-\gl H_v}\,e^{-\gl K_s\comp H_v}\bigr)\\ &= E_\xi\bigl(e^{-\gl H_v}\,E_\xi\bigl(e^{-\gl K_s\comp H_v}\cond \cF_{H_v}\bigr)\bigr)\\ &= E_\xi\bigl(e^{-\gl H_v}\bigr) E_v\bigl(e^{-\gl K_s}\bigr), \end{align*} Integrating the last identity against the exponential law in the variable $s$, we find with formula~\eqref{eq1.14} \begin{equation*} \hE_\xi\bigl(e^{-\gl\zeta_\gb}\bigr) = e_\gl(\xi)\,\hE_v\bigl(e^{-\gl \zeta_\gb}\bigr), \end{equation*} and the proof is finished.
nodes.section: 1.5 Killing via the Local Time at the Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Split the resolvent at $\zeta_\gb$, use Fubini and the strong Markov property at the stopping times $K_s$, then factor the Laplace transform at $H_v$.

nodes.name: Proof of the Walsh mean exit time
nodes.statement: Since by construction $W$ has infinite lifetime, $\TW_{v,\gep}$ is the hitting time of the set of the $n$ points with local coordinates $(k,\gep)$, $\kn$. Therefore, by the independence of the choice of the edge for the values of the excursion, it follows that under $P_v$ the stopping time $\TW_{v,\gep}$ has the same law as the hitting time of the point $\gep>0$ of a reflected Brownian motion on $\R_+$, starting at $0$. Thus the statement of the lemma follows from equation~\eqref{eq1.6}.
nodes.section: 2 The Walsh Process
nodes.statement_short: Reduce the exit time to the hitting time of $\gep$ by reflected Brownian motion and apply $E_x(H_{\{a,b\}})=(x-a)(b-x)$.

nodes.name: Proof of the elastic escape probability
nodes.statement: We may consider the Walsh process $W$ as being pathwise constructed from a standard Brownian motion $B$ on the real line as in the previous section, and we shall use the notations and conventions from there. Then it is clear that under $P_v$ and under $\hP_v$, $\TW_{v,\gep}$ has the same law as the hitting time of the point $\gep$ in $\R_+$ by the reflecting Brownian motion $|B|$ under $Q_0$, that is, as $H^B_{\{-\gep,\gep\}}$ of the Brownian motion $B$ itself under $Q_0$. Let $K^w$ denote the right continuous pseudo-inverse of $L^w$. For fixed $s\in\R_+$ we get \begin{equation*} \{K^w_s < \TW_{v,\gep}\} = \{L^w(\TW_{v,\gep})>s\}. \end{equation*} Hence \begin{align*} P_v\bigl(K^w_s < \TW_{v,\gep}\bigr) &= P_v\bigl(L^w(\TW_{v,\gep})>s\bigr)\\ &= Q_0\bigl(L^B(H^B_{\{-\gep,\gep\}})>s\bigr). \end{align*} In appendix~B of~\cite{BMMG0} is shown with the method in~\cite[Section~6.4]{KaSh91} that under $Q_0$ the random variable $L^B(H^B_{\{-\gep,\gep\}})$ is exponentially distributed with mean $\gep$. So we find \begin{equation*} P_v\bigl(K^w_s < \TW_{v,\gep}\bigr) = e^{-s/\gep}. \end{equation*} We integrate this relation against the exponential law with rate $\gb$ in the variable $s$, and obtain \begin{align*} \hP_v\bigl(\zeta_{\gb,0}>\TW_{v,\gep}\bigr) &= 1 - \gb\int_0^\infty e^{-\gb s}\,P_v\bigl(K^W_s < \TW_{v,\gep}\bigr)\,ds\\ &= \frac{1}{1+\gep\gb}. \end{align*} We used the fact that due to the continuity of the paths of $W$ we have $\zeta_{\gb,0}\ne \TW_{v,\gep}$.
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.statement_short: Compare $\{K^w_s<\TW_{v,\gep}\}$ with $\{L^w(\TW_{v,\gep})>s\}$, use exponentiality of $L^B(H^B_{\{-\gep,\gep\}})$, and integrate against the killing law.

nodes.name: Proof of the elastic lifetime Laplace transform
nodes.statement: As remarked before, we may consider $L^w$ to be equal to the local time at the origin of the Brownian motion $B$ underlying the construction of $W$, and therefore the analogous statement is true for the right continuous pseudo-inverse $K^w$ of $L^w$. As above let $K^B$ denote the right continuous pseudo-inverse of $L^B$ (cf.~\ref{ssect1.2}). Then for $s\in\R_+$, \begin{align*} E_v\bigl(e^{-\gl K^w_s}\bigr) &= E^Q_0\bigl(e^{-\gl K^B_s}\bigr)\\ &= e^{-\sgl s}, \end{align*} where we used lemma~\ref{lem1.2}. Hence \begin{equation*} \hE_v\bigl(e^{-\gl \zeta_{\gb,0}}\bigr) = \gb \int_0^\infty e^{-(\gb+\sgl) t}\,dt, \end{equation*} which proves the lemma.
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.statement_short: Identify $K^w$ with $K^B$, use lemma 1.2, then integrate against the exponential law.

nodes.name: Proof of the sticky exit time identity
nodes.statement: Let $W$, and therefore also $\Ws$, start in the vertex $v$. Since $\Ws$ and $W$ have continuous paths with infinite lifetime we have for all $\gg\ge 0$ \begin{equation*} \TsW_{v,\gep} = \inf\bigl\{t>0,\, d(v,W_{\tau(t)})=\gep\bigr\}, \end{equation*} and in particular for $\gg=0$, \begin{equation*} \TW_{v,\gep} = \inf\bigl\{t>0,\, d(v,W_t)=\gep\bigr\}. \end{equation*} Moreover, as argued above, both infima are a.s.\ finite. Set \begin{equation*} \gs = \TW_{v,\gep} + \gg\,L^w_{\TW_{v,\gep}}. \end{equation*} Then $\tau(\gs) = \TW_{v,\gep}$, and therefore \begin{align*} d\bigl(v, \Ws_\gs\bigr) &= d\bigl(v, W_{\tau(\gs)}\bigr)\\ &= d\bigl(v, W_{\TW_{v,\gep}}\bigr)\\ &= \gep. \end{align*} Consequently we get $\TsW_{v,\gep} \le \gs$. To derive the converse inequality we remark that \begin{align*} \gep &= d\bigl(v, \Ws_{\TsW_{v,\gep}}\bigr)\\ &= d\bigl(v, W_{\tau(\TsW_{v,\gep})}\bigr), \end{align*} which implies \begin{equation*} \tau\bigl(\TsW_{v,\gep}\bigr)\ge \TW_{v,\gep}. \end{equation*} Since $\tau$ is strictly increasing this entails \begin{equation*} \TsW_{v,\gep} \ge \tau^{-1}\bigl(\TW_{v,\gep}\bigr) = \gs, \end{equation*} and the proof is finished.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Two-sided inequality: exhibit $\gs=\TW_{v,\gep}+\gg L^w_{\TW_{v,\gep}}$ with $\tau(\gs)=\TW_{v,\gep}$, then use strict monotonicity of $\tau$ for the converse.

nodes.name: Proof of the sticky mean exit time
nodes.statement: By construction, the paths of $W$ starting in $v$ hit the complement of $B_\gep(v)$ exactly when the underlying standard Brownian motion $B$ (cf.\ section~\ref{sect2}) starting at the origin hits one of the points $\pm\gep$ on the real line. Thus under $P_v$, $L^w(\TW_{v,\gep})$ has the same law as $L^B(H^B_{\{-\gep,\gep\}})$ under $P_0$. Lemma~\ref{lem1.3} states that under $P_0$ this random variable is exponentially distributed with mean $\gep$. Then equation~\eqref{eq4.6} follows directly from lemmas~\ref{lem4.3}, and \ref{lem2.1}.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Transfer the law of $L^w(\TW_{v,\gep})$ to $L^B(H^B_{\{-\gep,\gep\}})$, which is exponential with mean $\gep$, then apply lemmas 4.3 and 2.1.

nodes.name: Proof of the sticky generator theorem
nodes.statement: Let $w_k$, $\kn$, and $\gg$ be defined as in~\eqref{eq4.4}, and note that due to the condition~\eqref{eq1.1a} on $b_k$, $\kn$, and $c$, we have $w_k\in [0,1]$, $\kn$, $\sum_k w_k =1$, as well as $\gg>0$. Hence we can construct the associated sticky Walsh process $\Ws$ as above. Let $A^s$ denote the generator of $\Ws$ with domain $\cD(A^s)$. Then we have for $f\in\cD(A^s)$, $A^s f(v) = 1/2 f''(v)$ (cf.\ theorem~\ref{thm_Feller}). On the other hand, we can compute $A^s f(v)$ via Dynkin's formula as follows \begin{align*} A^s f(v) &= \lim_{\gep\da 0} \frac{E_v\Bigl(f\bigl(\Ws(\TsW_{v,\gep})\bigr)\Bigr)-f(v)} {E_v\bigl(\TsW_{v,\gep}\bigr)}\\[1ex] &= \lim_{\gep\da 0} \frac{\sum_k w_k f_k(\gep) - f(v)}{\gep^2 + \gg\gep}, \end{align*} where we used corollary~\ref{cor4.4}. Since the directional derivatives of $f$ at $v$ \begin{equation*} f'(v_k)=\lim_{\xi\to v,\,\xi\in l_k} \frac{f(\xi)-f(v)}{d(\xi,v)},\qquad k\in\sn, \end{equation*} exist (cf.\ lemma~\ref{lemC02}), we obviously get the boundary condition \begin{equation} \frac{1}{2}\,f''(v) = \frac{1}{\gg}\,\sum_{k=1}^n w_k f'(v_k) \end{equation} as a necessary condition. Finally, inserting of the values~\eqref{eq4.4} of the parameters $w_k$, $\kn$, and $\gg$ into equation~\eqref{eq4.7} we complete the proof of theorem~\ref{thm4.2}.

nodes.statement_short: Evaluate $A^sf(v)$ by Dynkin's formula with $E_v(\TsW_{v,\gep})=\gep^2+\gg\gep$ and read off the boundary condition.

nodes.name: Proof of the sticky second-derivative formula
nodes.statement: Let $A^s$ be the generator of $\Ws$ on $\Co$. From the identity $A^s \RsW_\gl = \gl\,\RsW_\gl -\text{id}$, and the definition of $\tau$ we get \begin{align*} \frac{1}{2}\,\bigl(\RsW_\gl f\bigr)''(v) &= \gl E_v\Bigl(\int_0^\infty e^{-\gl t}\bigl(f(\Ws_t)-f(v)\bigr)\,dt\Bigr)\\ &= \gl E_v\Bigl(\int_0^\infty e^{-\gl(s+\gg L^w_s)} \bigl(f(W_s)-f(v)\bigr)\,(ds + \gg dL^w_s)\Bigr)\\ &= \gl E_v\Bigl(\int_0^\infty e^{-\gl(s+\gg L^w_s)} \bigl(f(W_s)-f(v)\bigr)\,ds \Bigr). \end{align*} In the last equality we used the fact that $L^w$ only grows when $W$ is at the vertex~$v$. By construction of the Walsh process $W$ we have \begin{align*} E_v\Bigl(&e^{-\gl\gg L^w_s}\bigl(f(W_s)-f(v)\bigr)\Bigr)\\ &= \sum_{k=1}^n w_k\,E_0\Bigl(e^{-\gl\gg L^B_s} \bigl(f_k(|B_s|) - f_k(0)\bigr) \Bigr)\\ &= 2\sum_{k=1}^n w_k \int_0^\infty \int_0^\infty e^{-\gl\gg y} \bigl(f_k(x) - f_k(0)\bigr)\,\frac{x+y}{\sqrt{2\pi s^3}}\, e^{-(x+y)^2/2s}\,dx\,dy, \end{align*} where we used lemma~\ref{lem1.1}. We insert the last expression above, and use formula~\eqref{LT}. This gives \begin{align*} \frac{1}{2}\,\bigl(\RsW_\gl f\bigr)''(v) &= 2\gl \sum_{k=1}^n w_k\,\frac{1}{\sgl + \gg\gl}\, \int_0^\infty e^{-\sgl x}\bigl(f_k(x)-f_k(0)\bigr)\,dx\\ &= \frac{1}{\sgl+\gg\gl}\,\bigl(2\gl\,(e^w_\gl,f) - \sgl f(v)\bigr). \qedhere \end{align*}

nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the resolvent in the $W$ time scale, apply the joint law of $(|B_s|,L^B_s)$, and integrate with the stable-$1/2$ Laplace transform.

nodes.name: Proof of the inverse-local-time relation
nodes.statement: For $\gg$, $r\in\R_+$ define the random subset \begin{equation*} J_\gg(r) = \{t\ge 0,\, L^s_t>r\} \end{equation*} of $\R_+$. Since $L^s$ is pathwise increasing, this set is a random interval with endpoints $K^s_r$ and $+\infty$. The relation $L^s_{K^s_r}=r$ implies that \begin{equation*} J_\gg(r) = (K^s_r,+\infty). \end{equation*} In particular, we have $J_0 = (K^w_r,+\infty)$. Now \begin{equation*} t\in J_\gg(r) \Leftrightarrow L^s_t = L^w_{\tau(t)} > r \Leftrightarrow \tau(t)\in J_0(r). \end{equation*} In other words, $J_\gg(r) = \tau^{-1}\bigl(J_0(r))$, and therefore $K^s_r=\tau^{-1}(K^w_r)$ holds. From the definition of $\tau^{-1}$ (see equation~\eqref{eq4.1}), and the relation $L^s_{K^s_r}=r$ we obtain formula~\eqref{eq5.1a}

nodes.statement_short: Identify the random interval $J_\gg(r)=\{L^s>r\}$ as $\tau^{-1}(J_0(r))$, so $K^s_r=\tau^{-1}(K^w_r)=K^w_r+\gg r$.

nodes.name: Proof of the general lifetime Laplace transform
nodes.statement: With corollary~\ref{cor5.1b} and $\zeta_{\gb,\gg} = K^s_S$ we obtain \begin{align*} \hE_v\bigl(e^{-\gl \zeta_{\gb,\gg}}\bigr) &= \gb \int_0^\infty E_v\bigl(e^{-\gl K^s_r}\bigr)\,e^{-\gb r}\,dr\\ &= \frac{\gb}{\gb + \sgl + \gg \gl}. \qedhere \end{align*}
nodes.section: 5 The General Brownian Motion on a Single Vertex Graph
nodes.statement_short: Integrate $E_v(e^{-\gl K^s_r})=e^{-(\sqrt{2\gl}+\gg\gl)r}$ against the exponential law of rate $\gb$.

nodes.name: Proof of the general generator theorem
nodes.statement: As in the previous cases it is readily seen that the definition~\eqref{eq5.5a} of the parameters $\gg$, $\gb$, $w_k$, $\kn$, is consistent with the conditions used in the above construction of $\Wg$. Let $A^g$ be the generator of $\Wg$ with domain $\cD(A^g)$. Since $\Wg$ is a Brownian motion on $\cG$ in the sense of definition~\ref{def_BM}, it follows from theorem~\ref{thm_Feller} that $\cD(A^g)\subset \Cii$, and that for all $f\in\cD(A^g)$, $A^g f(\xi) = 1/2\,f''(\xi)$, $\xi\in\cG$. Let $h\in\Co$, $\gl>0$. Then $\Rg_\gl h\in\cD(A^g)$, and therefore we may compute with equation~\eqref{eq5.4} as follows \begin{align*} \frac{\gg}{2}\,\bigl(\Rg_\gl h\bigr)''(v) &= \frac{\gg}{2}\,\bigl(\RsW_\gl h\bigr)''(v) - \gb\,\rho(\gl)\,2\gl \bigl(\RsW_\gl h\bigr)(v)\\ &= \sum_{k=1}^n w_k\,\bigl(\RsW_\gl h\bigr)'(v_k) - \gb\,\rho(\gl)\,\gg\gl \bigl(\RsW_\gl h\bigr)(v), \end{align*} where we used the fact that, since $\RsW_\gl h$ is in the domain of the generator $A^s$ of $\Ws$, it satisfies the boundary condition~\eqref{eq4.7}. We rewrite this equation in the following way: \begin{equation} \begin{split} \frac{\gg}{2}\,\bigl(\Rg_\gl h\bigr)''(v) = \sum_{k=1}^n w_k\,\bigl(\RsW_\gl h\bigr)'(v_k) &+\gb\sgl\,\rho(\gl) \bigl(\RsW_\gl h\bigr)(v)\\ &-\gb\,\rho(\gl)\bigl(\sgl+\gg\gl\bigr)\,\bigl(\RsW_\gl h\Bigr)(v). \end{split} \end{equation} Now we differentiate equation~\eqref{eq5.4} at $\xi\in l_k$, $\kn$, let $\xi$ tend to $v$ along any edge $l_k$, and sum the resulting equation against the weights $w_k$, $\kn$. Then we get the following formula \begin{equation} \sum_{k=1}^n w_k\,\bigl(\Rg_\gl h\bigr)'(v_k) = \sum_{k=1}^n w_k\,\bigl(\RsW_\gl h\bigr)'(v_k) + \gb\sgl\,\rho(\gl)\bigl(\RsW_\gl h\bigr)(v), \end{equation} where we used $\sum_k w_k=1$. On the other hand, for $\xi=v$, equation~\eqref{eq5.4} gives \begin{equation} \bigl(\Rg_\gl h\bigr)(v) = \rho(\gl)\bigl(\sgl +\gg\gl\bigr)\bigl(\RsW_\gl h\bigr)(v). \end{equation} A comparison of equations~\eqref{eq5.6}, \eqref{eq5.7} with \eqref{eq5.5} shows that we have proved the following formula \begin{equation} \frac{\gg}{2}\,\bigl(\Rg_\gl h\bigr)''(v) = \sum_{k=1}^n w_k\,\bigl(\Rg_\gl h\bigr)'(v_k) - \gb \bigl(\Rg_\gl h\bigr)(v). \end{equation} With the values~\eqref{eq5.5a} for $\gb$, $\gg$, and $w_k$, $\kn$, it is obvious that $f=\Rg_\gl h$ satisfies equation~\eqref{eq1.1b}. Since $\Rg_\gl$ is surjective from $\Co$ onto the domain of the generator $A^g$ of $\Wg$, the proof of the theorem is finished.
