nodes.statement_short: Use that $L^B(H^B_{\{-\gep,\gep\}})$ is exponential with mean $\gep$ to get $e^{-s/\gep}$.

nodes.name: Integrate against the killing law
nodes.statement: We integrate this relation against the exponential law with rate $\gb$ in the variable $s$, and obtain \begin{align*} \hP_v\bigl(\zeta_{\gb,0}>\TW_{v,\gep}\bigr) &= 1 - \gb\int_0^\infty e^{-\gb s}\,P_v\bigl(K^W_s < \TW_{v,\gep}\bigr)\,ds\\ &= \frac{1}{1+\gep\gb}. \end{align*} We used the fact that due to the continuity of the paths of $W$ we have $\zeta_{\gb,0}\ne \TW_{v,\gep}$.
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.statement_short: Integrating $e^{-s/\gep}$ against rate-$\gb$ exponential yields $(1+\gep\gb)^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Identify $K^w$ with the Brownian inverse local time
nodes.statement: As remarked before, we may consider $L^w$ to be equal to the local time at the origin of the Brownian motion $B$ underlying the construction of $W$, and therefore the analogous statement is true for the right continuous pseudo-inverse $K^w$ of $L^w$. As above let $K^B$ denote the right continuous pseudo-inverse of $L^B$ (cf.~\ref{ssect1.2}).
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the pseudo-inverse $K^B$ of $L^B$.

nodes.name: Apply the Laplace transform of $K^B_s$
nodes.statement: Then for $s\in\R_+$, \begin{align*} E_v\bigl(e^{-\gl K^w_s}\bigr) &= E^Q_0\bigl(e^{-\gl K^B_s}\bigr)\\ &= e^{-\sgl s}, \end{align*} where we used lemma~\ref{lem1.2}.
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 1.2 gives $E_v(e^{-\gl K^w_s}) = e^{-\sqrt{2\gl}s}$.

nodes.name: Integrate against the exponential law
nodes.statement: Hence \begin{equation*} \hE_v\bigl(e^{-\gl \zeta_{\gb,0}}\bigr) = \gb \int_0^\infty e^{-(\gb+\sgl) t}\,dt, \end{equation*} which proves the lemma.
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.statement_short: Integrating over $s$ gives $\gb/(\gb+\sqrt{2\gl})$.

nodes.name: Write both exit times as infima
nodes.statement: Let $W$, and therefore also $\Ws$, start in the vertex $v$. Since $\Ws$ and $W$ have continuous paths with infinite lifetime we have for all $\gg\ge 0$ \begin{equation*} \TsW_{v,\gep} = \inf\bigl\{t>0,\, d(v,W_{\tau(t)})=\gep\bigr\}, \end{equation*} and in particular for $\gg=0$, \begin{equation*} \TW_{v,\gep} = \inf\bigl\{t>0,\, d(v,W_t)=\gep\bigr\}. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Express $\TsW_{v,\gep}$ and $\TW_{v,\gep}$ through the distance to $v$.

nodes.name: Introduce the candidate time $\gs$
nodes.statement: Moreover, as argued above, both infima are a.s.\ finite. Set \begin{equation*} \gs = \TW_{v,\gep} + \gg\,L^w_{\TW_{v,\gep}}. \end{equation*} Then $\tau(\gs) = \TW_{v,\gep}$, and therefore
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Set $\gs = \TW_{v,\gep}+\gg L^w_{\TW_{v,\gep}}$, so that $\tau(\gs)=\TW_{v,\gep}$.

nodes.name: Prove $\TsW_{v,\gep}\le\gs$
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} d\bigl(v, \Ws_\gs\bigr) &= d\bigl(v, W_{\tau(\gs)}\bigr)\\ &= d\bigl(v, W_{\TW_{v,\gep}}\bigr)\\ &= \gep. \end{align*} Consequently we get $\TsW_{v,\gep} \le \gs$.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Show $d(v,\Ws_\gs)=\gep$.

nodes.name: Prove the converse inequality and conclude
nodes.statement: To derive the converse inequality we remark that \begin{align*} \gep &= d\bigl(v, \Ws_{\TsW_{v,\gep}}\bigr)\\ &= d\bigl(v, W_{\tau(\TsW_{v,\gep})}\bigr), \end{align*} which implies \begin{equation*} \tau\bigl(\TsW_{v,\gep}\bigr)\ge \TW_{v,\gep}. \end{equation*} Since $\tau$ is strictly increasing this entails \begin{equation*} \TsW_{v,\gep} \ge \tau^{-1}\bigl(\TW_{v,\gep}\bigr) = \gs, \end{equation*} and the proof is finished.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Strict monotonicity of $\tau$ gives $\TsW_{v,\gep}\ge\gs$.

nodes.name: Transfer the local time law to the real line
nodes.statement: By construction, the paths of $W$ starting in $v$ hit the complement of $B_\gep(v)$ exactly when the underlying standard Brownian motion $B$ (cf.\ section~\ref{sect2}) starting at the origin hits one of the points $\pm\gep$ on the real line. Thus under $P_v$, $L^w(\TW_{v,\gep})$ has the same law as $L^B(H^B_{\{-\gep,\gep\}})$ under $P_0$.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: $L^w(\TW_{v,\gep})$ has the law of $L^B(H^B_{\{-\gep,\gep\}})$.

nodes.name: Invoke exponentiality of the local time
nodes.statement: Lemma~\ref{lem1.3} states that under $P_0$ this random variable is exponentially distributed with mean $\gep$.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 1.3 gives mean $\gep$.

nodes.name: Combine with lemmas 4.3 and 2.1
nodes.statement: Then equation~\eqref{eq4.6} follows directly from lemmas~\ref{lem4.3}, and \ref{lem2.1}.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Add $\gep^2$ and $\gg\gep$ to obtain the mean exit time.

nodes.name: Check consistency of the parameters
nodes.statement: Let $w_k$, $\kn$, and $\gg$ be defined as in~\eqref{eq4.4}, and note that due to the condition~\eqref{eq1.1a} on $b_k$, $\kn$, and $c$, we have $w_k\in [0,1]$, $\kn$, $\sum_k w_k =1$, as well as $\gg>0$. Hence we can construct the associated sticky Walsh process $\Ws$ as above.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Verify $w_k\in[0,1]$, $\sum_k w_k=1$, $\gg>0$ so that $\Ws$ can be constructed.

nodes.name: Recall the generator acts as $\tfrac12 f''$
nodes.statement: Let $A^s$ denote the generator of $\Ws$ with domain $\cD(A^s)$. Then we have for $f\in\cD(A^s)$, $A^s f(v) = 1/2 f''(v)$ (cf.\ theorem~\ref{thm_Feller}).
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Feller's theorem gives $A^sf(v)=\tfrac12 f''(v)$.

nodes.name: Compute $A^sf(v)$ by Dynkin's formula
nodes.statement: On the other hand, we can compute $A^s f(v)$ via Dynkin's formula as follows \begin{align*} A^s f(v) &= \lim_{\gep\da 0} \frac{E_v\Bigl(f\bigl(\Ws(\TsW_{v,\gep})\bigr)\Bigr)-f(v)} {E_v\bigl(\TsW_{v,\gep}\bigr)}\\[1ex] &= \lim_{\gep\da 0} \frac{\sum_k w_k f_k(\gep) - f(v)}{\gep^2 + \gg\gep}, \end{align*} where we used corollary~\ref{cor4.4}.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Insert $E_v(\TsW_{v,\gep})=\gep^2+\gg\gep$ from corollary 4.4.

nodes.name: Take the limit to obtain the boundary condition
nodes.statement: Since the directional derivatives of $f$ at $v$ \begin{equation*} f'(v_k)=\lim_{\xi\to v,\,\xi\in l_k} \frac{f(\xi)-f(v)}{d(\xi,v)},\qquad k\in\sn, \end{equation*} exist (cf.\ lemma~\ref{lemC02}), we obviously get the boundary condition \begin{equation} \frac{1}{2}\,f''(v) = \frac{1}{\gg}\,\sum_{k=1}^n w_k f'(v_k) \end{equation} as a necessary condition.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Existence of $f'(v_k)$ yields $\tfrac12 f''(v)=\tfrac1\gg\sum_k w_kf'(v_k)$.

nodes.name: Substitute the parameter values
nodes.statement: Finally, inserting of the values~\eqref{eq4.4} of the parameters $w_k$, $\kn$, and $\gg$ into equation~\eqref{eq4.7} we complete the proof of theorem~\ref{thm4.2}.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Inserting $w_k=b_k/(1-c)$, $\gg=c/(1-c)$ gives condition (1.1b).

nodes.name: Expand the resolvent in the $W$ time scale
nodes.statement: Let $A^s$ be the generator of $\Ws$ on $\Co$. From the identity $A^s \RsW_\gl = \gl\,\RsW_\gl -\text{id}$, and the definition of $\tau$ we get \begin{align*} \frac{1}{2}\,\bigl(\RsW_\gl f\bigr)''(v) &= \gl E_v\Bigl(\int_0^\infty e^{-\gl t}\bigl(f(\Ws_t)-f(v)\bigr)\,dt\Bigr)\\ &= \gl E_v\Bigl(\int_0^\infty e^{-\gl(s+\gg L^w_s)} \bigl(f(W_s)-f(v)\bigr)\,(ds + \gg dL^w_s)\Bigr)\\ &= \gl E_v\Bigl(\int_0^\infty e^{-\gl(s+\gg L^w_s)} \bigl(f(W_s)-f(v)\bigr)\,ds \Bigr). \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Use $A^s\RsW_\gl=\gl\RsW_\gl-\mathrm{id}$ and the definition of $\tau$.

nodes.name: Drop the $dL^w$ term
nodes.statement: In the last equality we used the fact that $L^w$ only grows when $W$ is at the vertex~$v$.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: $L^w$ grows only at the vertex, where the integrand vanishes.

nodes.name: Apply the joint law of $(|B_s|,L^B_s)$
nodes.statement: By construction of the Walsh process $W$ we have \begin{align*} E_v\Bigl(&e^{-\gl\gg L^w_s}\bigl(f(W_s)-f(v)\bigr)\Bigr)\\ &= \sum_{k=1}^n w_k\,E_0\Bigl(e^{-\gl\gg L^B_s} \bigl(f_k(|B_s|) - f_k(0)\bigr) \Bigr)\\ &= 2\sum_{k=1}^n w_k \int_0^\infty \int_0^\infty e^{-\gl\gg y} \bigl(f_k(x) - f_k(0)\bigr)\,\frac{x+y}{\sqrt{2\pi s^3}}\, e^{-(x+y)^2/2s}\,dx\,dy, \end{align*} where we used lemma~\ref{lem1.1}.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the expectation as a double integral using lemma 1.1.

nodes.name: Integrate with the stable-$1/2$ Laplace transform
nodes.statement: We insert the last expression above, and use formula~\eqref{LT}. This gives \begin{align*} \frac{1}{2}\,\bigl(\RsW_\gl f\bigr)''(v) &= 2\gl \sum_{k=1}^n w_k\,\frac{1}{\sgl + \gg\gl}\, \int_0^\infty e^{-\sgl x}\bigl(f_k(x)-f_k(0)\bigr)\,dx\\ &= \frac{1}{\sgl+\gg\gl}\,\bigl(2\gl\,(e^w_\gl,f) - \sgl f(v)\bigr). \qedhere \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Formula (LT) gives the factor $(\sqrt{2\gl}+\gg\gl)^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Describe the level set of $L^s$ as an interval
nodes.statement: For $\gg$, $r\in\R_+$ define the random subset \begin{equation*} J_\gg(r) = \{t\ge 0,\, L^s_t>r\} \end{equation*} of $\R_+$. Since $L^s$ is pathwise increasing, this set is a random interval with endpoints $K^s_r$ and $+\infty$. The relation $L^s_{K^s_r}=r$ implies that \begin{equation*} J_\gg(r) = (K^s_r,+\infty). \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 5 The General Brownian Motion on a Single Vertex Graph
nodes.statement_short: Monotonicity gives $J_\gg(r)=(K^s_r,+\infty)$.

nodes.name: Relate $J_\gg(r)$ to $J_0(r)$ through $\tau$
nodes.statement: In particular, we have $J_0 = (K^w_r,+\infty)$. Now \begin{equation*} t\in J_\gg(r) \Leftrightarrow L^s_t = L^w_{\tau(t)} > r \Leftrightarrow \tau(t)\in J_0(r). \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 5 The General Brownian Motion on a Single Vertex Graph
nodes.statement_short: $t\in J_\gg(r)\Leftrightarrow \tau(t)\in J_0(r)$.

nodes.name: Invert $\tau$ and conclude
nodes.statement: In other words, $J_\gg(r) = \tau^{-1}\bigl(J_0(r))$, and therefore $K^s_r=\tau^{-1}(K^w_r)$ holds. From the definition of $\tau^{-1}$ (see equation~\eqref{eq4.1}), and the relation $L^s_{K^s_r}=r$ we obtain formula~\eqref{eq5.1a}
nodes.section: 5 The General Brownian Motion on a Single Vertex Graph
nodes.statement_short: $K^s_r=\tau^{-1}(K^w_r)=K^w_r+\gg r$.

nodes.name: Check parameter consistency
nodes.statement: As in the previous cases it is readily seen that the definition~\eqref{eq5.5a} of the parameters $\gg$, $\gb$, $w_k$, $\kn$, is consistent with the conditions used in the above construction of $\Wg$.
nodes.section: 5 The General Brownian Motion on a Single Vertex Graph
nodes.statement_short: The choices (5.5a) satisfy the constraints of the construction.

nodes.name: Set up the generator computation
nodes.statement: Let $A^g$ be the generator of $\Wg$ with domain $\cD(A^g)$. Since $\Wg$ is a Brownian motion on $\cG$ in the sense of definition~\ref{def_BM}, it follows from theorem~\ref{thm_Feller} that $\cD(A^g)\subset \Cii$, and that for all $f\in\cD(A^g)$, $A^g f(\xi) = 1/2\,f''(\xi)$, $\xi\in\cG$. Let $h\in\Co$, $\gl>0$. Then $\Rg_\gl h\in\cD(A^g)$, and therefore we may compute with equation~\eqref{eq5.4} as follows
nodes.section: 5 The General Brownian Motion on a Single Vertex Graph
nodes.statement_short: Feller's theorem gives $\cD(A^g)\subset\Cii$ and $A^gf=\tfrac12 f''$.

nodes.name: Differentiate the resolvent identity twice at $v$
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} \frac{\gg}{2}\,\bigl(\Rg_\gl h\bigr)''(v) &= \frac{\gg}{2}\,\bigl(\RsW_\gl h\bigr)''(v) - \gb\,\rho(\gl)\,2\gl \bigl(\RsW_\gl h\bigr)(v)\\ &= \sum_{k=1}^n w_k\,\bigl(\RsW_\gl h\bigr)'(v_k) - \gb\,\rho(\gl)\,\gg\gl \bigl(\RsW_\gl h\bigr)(v), \end{align*} where we used the fact that, since $\RsW_\gl h$ is in the domain of the generator $A^s$ of $\Ws$, it satisfies the boundary condition~\eqref{eq4.7}.
nodes.section: 5 The General Brownian Motion on a Single Vertex Graph
nodes.statement_short: Use that $\RsW_\gl h$ satisfies the sticky boundary condition (4.7).

nodes.name: Rearrange into the key identity
nodes.statement: We rewrite this equation in the following way: \begin{equation} \begin{split} \frac{\gg}{2}\,\bigl(\Rg_\gl h\bigr)''(v) = \sum_{k=1}^n w_k\,\bigl(\RsW_\gl h\bigr)'(v_k) &+\gb\sgl\,\rho(\gl) \bigl(\RsW_\gl h\bigr)(v)\\ &-\gb\,\rho(\gl)\bigl(\sgl+\gg\gl\bigr)\,\bigl(\RsW_\gl h\Bigr)(v). \end{split} \end{equation}
nodes.section: 5 The General Brownian Motion on a Single Vertex Graph
nodes.statement_short: Split the $\gb\rho(\gl)$ term into $\sqrt{2\gl}$ and $\sqrt{2\gl}+\gg\gl$ pieces.

nodes.name: Compute the weighted first derivatives
nodes.statement: Now we differentiate equation~\eqref{eq5.4} at $\xi\in l_k$, $\kn$, let $\xi$ tend to $v$ along any edge $l_k$, and sum the resulting equation against the weights $w_k$, $\kn$. Then we get the following formula \begin{equation} \sum_{k=1}^n w_k\,\bigl(\Rg_\gl h\bigr)'(v_k) = \sum_{k=1}^n w_k\,\bigl(\RsW_\gl h\bigr)'(v_k) + \gb\sgl\,\rho(\gl)\bigl(\RsW_\gl h\bigr)(v), \end{equation} where we used $\sum_k w_k=1$.
nodes.section: 5 The General Brownian Motion on a Single Vertex Graph
nodes.statement_short: Differentiate (5.4) along each edge and sum against $w_k$.

nodes.name: Evaluate at the vertex
nodes.statement: On the other hand, for $\xi=v$, equation~\eqref{eq5.4} gives \begin{equation} \bigl(\Rg_\gl h\bigr)(v) = \rho(\gl)\bigl(\sgl +\gg\gl\bigr)\bigl(\RsW_\gl h\bigr)(v). \end{equation}
nodes.section: 5 The General Brownian Motion on a Single Vertex Graph
nodes.statement_short: Obtain $(\Rg_\gl h)(v)=\rho(\gl)(\sqrt{2\gl}+\gg\gl)(\RsW_\gl h)(v)$.

nodes.name: Compare and conclude
nodes.statement: A comparison of equations~\eqref{eq5.6}, \eqref{eq5.7} with \eqref{eq5.5} shows that we have proved the following formula \begin{equation} \frac{\gg}{2}\,\bigl(\Rg_\gl h\bigr)''(v) = \sum_{k=1}^n w_k\,\bigl(\Rg_\gl h\bigr)'(v_k) - \gb \bigl(\Rg_\gl h\bigr)(v). \end{equation} With the values~\eqref{eq5.5a} for $\gb$, $\gg$, and $w_k$, $\kn$, it is obvious that $f=\Rg_\gl h$ satisfies equation~\eqref{eq1.1b}. Since $\Rg_\gl$ is surjective from $\Co$ onto the domain of the generator $A^g$ of $\Wg$, the proof of the theorem is finished.
nodes.section: 5 The General Brownian Motion on a Single Vertex Graph
nodes.statement_short: The comparison gives (5.8), which is exactly condition (1.1b) for $f=\Rg_\gl h$.
